title: Caddyshack
logline: Chaos at an upscale golf club. Loose ensemble comedy with improvised riffs.
overview: At an exclusive country club, an ambitious young caddy, Danny Noonan, eagerly pursues a caddy scholarship in hopes of attending college and, in turn, avoiding a job at the lumber yard. In order to succeed, he must first win the favour of the elitist Judge Smails, and then the caddy golf tournament which Smails sponsors.

jokes.text: Danny saw me naked! / You think you're cool, Danny.
jokes.setup: Chaotic Noonan household morning rush with kids shouting over each other
jokes.punchline: A sibling tattles that Danny saw them naked, then immediately pivots to a withering social judgment — 'You think you're cool, Danny' — delivered with absurd conviction
jokes.explanation: The two-beat combo — accusation then social verdict — is a sharp little piece of kid logic comedy. The quick escalation from outrage to condescension is funny but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Did you brush your teeth? / Both of them.
jokes.setup: Mom asks routine parenting question about dental hygiene
jokes.punchline: 'Both of them' — implying Danny only has two teeth, delivered with complete matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words do enormous work. The setup is completely mundane, the punchline recontextualizes it as a poverty/neglect joke without being cruel. Classic setup/punchline with great structure. Among the stronger jokes in this reel.

jokes.text: The Douglases got fake brick. You don't have to paint it.
jokes.setup: Dad tells the kids they need to paint the house when they get back from Little League
jokes.punchline: Kid offers 'The Douglases got fake brick' as a sincere labor-saving solution — an absurdly practical deflection from chores
jokes.explanation: Good slice-of-life domestic humor. The kid's completely sincere logic is funny but doesn't land as hard as similar bits in this sequence.

jokes.text: I talked to a guy who went there. He said there were only two girls and they were both nuns.
jokes.setup: Parents push Danny toward the St. Copius scholarship as a college option
jokes.punchline: Danny reports his research: two girls, both nuns — a wry, deadpan demolition of the pitch
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. The escalation of 'two girls… both nuns' is a well-structured two-beat punchline. It characterizes Danny as a teenager prioritizing social life over academics while also being funny on its own terms.

jokes.text: How many cokes? / Four or five. / What are you, a diabetic?
jokes.setup: Mom interrogates Danny about how he spent his caddy money on lunch
jokes.punchline: 'What are you, a diabetic?' — a hyperbolic, slightly absurd parental overreaction to soda consumption
jokes.explanation: Classic overbearing-parent comedy. The specific medical diagnosis as punchline is a nice touch — funnier than a generic 'that's too much!' response. Good economy.

jokes.text: Do you take drugs? / Every day. / Good. So what's the problem?
jokes.setup: Danny tries to have a sincere life-advice conversation with Ty Webb; Ty, sensing something is off, asks if Danny takes drugs
jokes.punchline: Ty answers his own implicit follow-up — 'Good. So what's the problem?' — treating daily drug use as a baseline prerequisite for healthy functioning
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The joke only works because of who Ty Webb is — a wealthy, blissed-out zen golfer for whom daily drug use is simply the responsible adult baseline. The structure is a perfect three-beat: question, confession, normalized approval. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — sharp, unexpected, perfectly economical, and deeply character-specific. 'Good. So what's the problem?' is one of the most quotable lines in the film.

jokes.text: They said I should be a fire-watcher.
jokes.setup: Danny asks about the vocational aptitude test ('Cooter Preference Test') and what it recommended for Ty
jokes.punchline: 'They said I should be a fire-watcher' — an absurdly useless/passive vocation delivered with total serenity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Ty Webb. The vocation 'fire-watcher' captures the character's passive, contemplative nature in a single image. It also quietly implies that even a standardized test couldn't find a real use for him. High character integration.

jokes.text: What are you supposed to be? / An underachiever.
jokes.setup: Ty asks what Danny's aptitude test recommended for him
jokes.punchline: Danny deadpans 'An underachiever' — the test literally diagnosed his life situation, and he's stating it without irony
jokes.explanation: Good self-deprecating deadpan. The joke works as both character establishment and as a riff on the absurdity of vocational tests. Solid economy.

jokes.text: Oh, Danny, this isn't Russia. Is this Russia? This isn't Russia, is it? I didn't think so.
jokes.setup: Danny says he has to go to college, implying there's no other option
jokes.punchline: Ty breaks into a meandering, self-answering philosophical non-sequitur about whether this is Russia — as if that's the relevant issue — delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Ty Webb — the rambling, circular, Zen-koans-meets-stoned-libertarianism speech pattern. The self-answering rhetorical questions ('Is this Russia? This isn't Russia, is it? I didn't think so.') is a great comedic tic, and his confident conclusion ('No.') after talking himself in circles is perfectly absurd. High character integration.

jokes.text: I haven't even told him about the scholarship I didn't get. / What's wrong with lumber? I own two lumber yards. / I notice you don't spend too much time there. / I'm not sure where they are.
jokes.setup: Danny laments that he'll end up working in a lumber yard; Ty reveals he owns two lumber yards as if this validates the career path
jokes.punchline: Danny: 'I notice you don't spend too much time there.' Ty: 'I'm not sure where they are.' — Ty's wealth is so casual he's literally misplaced two lumber yards
jokes.explanation: One of the best Ty Webb jokes in the reel. The escalation is perfectly constructed: (1) Ty validates lumber work by revealing he owns lumber yards, (2) Danny calls him out for not being there, (3) Ty's response — 'I'm not sure where they are' — detonates the whole exchange. The joke only works for a character of Ty's specific disposition. The delivery of profound detachment toward things the audience knows should matter is classic Chevy Chase/Ty Webb and deeply character-integrated. Approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: I like you, Betty. / That's Danny, sir. / Danny.
jokes.setup: Ty is about to give Danny sincere life advice
jokes.punchline: He calls Danny 'Betty' — he doesn't know the kid's name despite having just caddied with him all morning
jokes.explanation: Good running characterization gag — Ty is too checked-out to remember anyone's name. The name 'Betty' is an especially funny choice. Part of a pattern. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Stop thinking. Let things happen. And be... the ball.
jokes.setup: Ty is giving Danny sincere-sounding life/golf philosophy
jokes.punchline: 'Be the ball' — the ultimate expression of Ty's golf mysticism, delivered with complete conviction as if it's profound wisdom
jokes.explanation: 'Be the ball' is the most culturally quotable line in this reel. It distills Ty Webb's character — New Age golf mysticism as life philosophy — into three words. The pause before 'the ball' is key to the delivery. High quotability score even if the craft of the joke itself is somewhat broader than the lumber yards exchange.

jokes.text: Be the ball, Danny. You're not being the ball, Danny.
jokes.setup: Ty has told Danny to be the ball and clear his mind; Danny is trying to putt
jokes.punchline: Ty breaks the zen silence with increasingly literal coaching instructions about being the ball, undermining the entire meditation exercise
jokes.explanation: The running gag payoff works beautifully — Ty coaches silence and emptiness while simultaneously breaking the silence with specific coaching. The self-contradiction is both philosophically absurd and deeply in character.

jokes.text: Well, it's kind of difficult with you talking like that. / I'm not talking. Stop talking.
jokes.setup: Danny calls out Ty for talking during the 'silence' meditation; Ty denies he's talking while continuing to talk
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not talking. Stop talking.' — Ty simultaneously denies talking and tells Danny to stop talking, in one breath
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. 'I'm not talking. Stop talking.' is a five-word contradiction that perfectly encapsulates Ty's total lack of self-awareness about his own behavior. The structure is elegant: accusation, denial, reversal of accusation — all in one sentence. Well above average for this reel.

jokes.text: Where did it go? / Right in the lumber yard. It's okay. We'll work on it.
jokes.setup: Danny tries Ty's 'be the ball' technique and hits a shot
jokes.punchline: The ball goes into 'the lumber yard' — a callback to Danny's lumber yard lament — delivered by Ty with gentle encouragement as if this is totally fine
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. 'Right in the lumber yard' works on two levels simultaneously — it's a golf term for rough/trees AND a direct callback to the earlier conversation about Danny's future. Ty's breezy 'We'll work on it' adds to the deadpan.

jokes.text: I think they're tunneling in from that construction site over yonder. / Czervik Construction Company? / I'll slap an injunction on them so fast it will make their heads spin!
jokes.setup: The greenskeeper reports gophers may be tunneling from a nearby construction site
jokes.punchline: Judge Smails immediately escalates to legal action — 'I'll slap an injunction on them so fast' — a wildly disproportionate response to gopher talk, perfectly characterizing his pompous litigiousness
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment for Judge Smails — his instinct to weaponize legal process against gophers tells you everything about him. Functional but not among the reel's best.

jokes.text: I'm looking at you. You wore green so you could hide.
jokes.setup: Ty is apparently mid-round commentary to someone (Mrs. Crane?) while caddying or playing
jokes.punchline: Ty accuses someone of wearing green to hide on the golf course — an absurd, paranoid, completely non-golf observation delivered as if it's cutting insight
jokes.explanation: Funny non-sequitur that fits Ty's pattern of confident, slightly paranoid observations. 'You wore green so you could hide' implies a level of premeditation on the part of a golf spectator that is delightfully absurd.

jokes.text: Mrs. Crane, you're a little monkey woman, you know that? You're a little monkey woman. You're lean and you're mean and you're not too far between either... I bet, are you, huh? Would you like to wrap your spikes around my head?
jokes.setup: Ty is apparently complimenting Mrs. Crane on her golf shot
jokes.punchline: His 'compliment' escalates from 'monkey woman' through 'lean and mean' to the deeply uncomfortable sexual innuendo of 'wrap your spikes around my head' — all delivered with Ty's characteristic breezy confidence
jokes.explanation: Classic Chevy Chase improvisational energy — the escalating 'compliment' that reveals Ty's complete social obliviousness. 'Monkey woman' as a term of endearment and the golf-spike sexual proposal are both deeply odd and character-perfect. The escalation structure elevates it.

jokes.text: I was unavoidably detained.
jokes.setup: Head groundskeeper Sandy is furious that Carl didn't cut the long grass on the 13th or mow the practice green
jokes.punchline: 'I was unavoidably detained' — Carl applies formal, legalistic language to whatever he was actually doing (implied: nothing, or something worse), with complete pompous sincerity
jokes.explanation: Bill Murray's delivery elevates a simple pompous-understatement joke. The formal vocabulary ('unavoidably detained') in Carl's voice is inherently funny. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Check me if I'm wrong, Sandy, but if I kill all the golfers, they're going to lock me up and throw away the key. / Gophers! Gophers! The little brown furry rodents!
jokes.setup: Sandy tells Carl to kill every gopher on the course
jokes.punchline: Carl mishears 'gophers' as 'golfers' and calmly walks through his legal jeopardy — implying he's given genuine thought to the feasibility of killing golfers — before Sandy has to frantically clarify
jokes.explanation: One of Bill Murray's best moments in the reel. The joke is a perfect Carl Spackler joke: he mishears, he doesn't panic at the misunderstanding, he carefully and reasonably explains why killing golfers might cause legal problems ('Check me if I'm wrong') — as if the core plan was otherwise sound. The logic of a dangerously unhinged man who is completely calm. 'Check me if I'm wrong, Sandy' is a great framing device. High character integration, excellent structure.

jokes.text: We can do that. We don't even have to have a reason.
jokes.setup: Sandy has clarified he means gophers, and tells Carl to kill them
jokes.punchline: 'We don't even have to have a reason' — Carl treats this like a legal/moral threshold he's relieved to have cleared, implying that for golfers he would have needed one
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to the golfer/gopher confusion. The implication that gopher killing requires no justification while golfer killing presumably would is darkly funny and perfectly in Carl's voice. 'We don't even have to have a reason' has a great rhythm. The escalation from joke 21 makes this land harder.

jokes.text: I'll just do the same thing, but with gophers.
jokes.setup: Sandy tells Carl to kill the gophers
jokes.punchline: Carl commits to doing 'the same thing' but with gophers — directly implying he has a pre-existing, apparently detailed plan for killing golfers that he will now simply redirect
jokes.explanation: Possibly the best single line in this reel. The economy is extraordinary — six words that retroactively confirm Carl has a detailed, standing protocol for killing golfers that he will simply apply to gophers. Bill Murray's delivery of this line with casual operational confidence is a perfect character moment. It's dark, specific, economical, and utterly irreplaceable. Approaches a 9+ for character integration.

jokes.text: It's not my fault nobody can understand what you're saying.
jokes.setup: Carl wraps up his conversation with Sandy
jokes.punchline: Carl blames Sandy (or the world) for not understanding him — a classic Murray ad-lib that breaks the fourth wall just enough to acknowledge his own character's incoherence
jokes.explanation: A decent throwaway line that's more of an ad-lib coda than a crafted joke. It's funny but slight.

jokes.text: So I jumped ship in Hong Kong and made my way over to Tibet and I get on as a looper at this course over in the Himalayas.
jokes.setup: Carl is apparently holding court with someone (a caddy?), launching into a rambling story with no apparent reason or connection to anything
jokes.punchline: The sheer bathos of 'jumped ship in Hong Kong… Tibet… Himalayas' as the preamble to a golf story — the global adventure is revealed to be about getting a caddy job
jokes.explanation: The opening of Carl's Dalai Lama monologue. Murray's rambling, authoritative delivery of increasingly absurd biography is funny in its own right. The setup is essentially Murray's voice and rhythm, which is high entertainment value.

jokes.text: The Dalai Lama, himself. The 12th son of the Lama. The flowing robes, the grace, bald, striking.
jokes.setup: Carl has set up that he got an impressive golf client
jokes.punchline: His description of the Dalai Lama — 'flowing robes, the grace, bald, striking' — is delivered as if reviewing a new golfer's physical attributes, reducing a spiritual icon to a golf-buddy assessment
jokes.explanation: The reduction of the Dalai Lama to a golf buddy ('bald, striking') is a great deflation of reverence. Murray's comma-separated physical assessment of a holy figure is perfectly absurd and deeply Carl.

jokes.text: He hauls off and whacks one. Big hitter, the Lama. Long!
jokes.setup: Carl describes the Dalai Lama's golf game
jokes.punchline: 'Big hitter, the Lama. Long!' — Carl is scouting the Dalai Lama as a golfer with the same serious assessment you'd give a touring pro, inverted syntax adding to the portentousness
jokes.explanation: The inverted syntax ('Big hitter, the Lama') is a great comic choice — it makes the assessment sound like a sportscast, treating the Dalai Lama as a subject of serious athletic analysis. Highly quotable and very Bill Murray.

jokes.text: Gunga-glalunga Gunga-gunga-da-gunga.
jokes.setup: Carl sets up 'do you know what the Lama says?' with great anticipation, as if quoting scripture
jokes.punchline: The Dalai Lama's golf-round wisdom turns out to be pure nonsense syllables — delivered by Murray with absolute conviction and appropriate weight
jokes.explanation: One of the great single-beat jokes in the film. The structure is impeccable: Carl builds enormous anticipation ('Do you know what the Lama says?'), then delivers complete nonsense with total gravitas. The gap between the solemnity of the setup and the absurdity of the punchline is massive. Murray's delivery makes the syllables sound meaningful while being meaningless. Easily the biggest laugh in the monologue and one of the reel's standout moments.

jokes.text: Oh, there won't be any money. But when you die on your deathbed, you will receive total consciousness.
jokes.setup: Carl confronts the Dalai Lama about payment for caddying 18 holes
jokes.punchline: The Lama offers 'total consciousness' on the deathbed instead of money — an absurd spiritual IOU that is simultaneously a commentary on New Age payment in spiritual currency vs. real wages
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic premise: the Dalai Lama stiffs a caddy and pays in posthumous enlightenment. The specificity of 'when you die on your deathbed' is funny — as opposed to, say, sometime before that. The joke works on multiple levels: deflating spiritual wisdom as cheap labor payment and characterizing Carl as the kind of guy who'd work for a holy man who can't tip.

jokes.text: So I've got that going for me. Which is nice.
jokes.setup: Carl has just explained he's going to receive 'total consciousness' on his deathbed instead of a caddy tip
jokes.punchline: 'So I've got that going for me. Which is nice.' — Carl treats posthumous enlightenment as a modest workplace perk, delivered with the mild satisfaction of someone noting a decent health plan
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the reel and one of the great lines in comedy film history. 'So I've got that going for me. Which is nice.' is the perfect deflation of the entire monologue and of cosmic spiritual promise. The gap between 'total consciousness' and 'which is nice' — the word 'nice' doing the work of acknowledging the promise while simultaneously reducing it to the level of a free parking spot — is a masterpiece of economy and bathos. Carl's complete sincerity and mild pleasure make it land even harder. This is a cultural touchstone, comparable to the 9.5/10 anchor example. The 'which is nice' has become one of the most-quoted lines in film comedy.

jokes.text: Lou raised the price of coke. He's been losing at the track.
jokes.setup: Danny is upset about the price of a coke going up to 50 cents
jokes.punchline: The explanation for the price hike is that Lou is losing at the track and passing the costs to the caddies — a corrupt, petty abuse of small power
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment for Lou — petty, self-serving, using his small kingdom to cover his gambling losses. Functional world-building comedy.

jokes.text: Well, I ain't paying no 50 cents for no coke! / Then you ain't getting no coke!
jokes.setup: Danny refuses to pay the inflated coke price
jokes.punchline: The double-negative standoff — 'I ain't paying no 50 cents for no coke!' met with 'Then you ain't getting no coke!' — is a perfect low-stakes class-war exchange
jokes.explanation: The parallel double-negative structure is funnier than the content. The mirror-image lines give it a nice rhythm. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: My friend, you have no idea how happy this is going to make me. / I'm going to enjoy this thoroughly. / I hope that means both of us. / Couldn't we just arm wrestle or something?
jokes.setup: Tony invites Danny outside for a fight
jokes.punchline: Danny's escalating de-escalation attempts — first 'I hope that means both of us' (hopeful), then 'Couldn't we just arm wrestle or something?' (desperate) — against Tony's mounting enthusiasm for violence
jokes.explanation: Good comic escalation with Danny's terror expressed through increasingly pathetic alternatives to fighting. 'Couldn't we just arm wrestle or something?' is a nice specific choice. Functional bully-comedy.

jokes.text: Whip his ass, Tony! / Now, who did you say the jerk was, jerk?
jokes.setup: Tony's brother arrives to help Tony beat up Danny; Tony confidently asks who Danny called a jerk
jokes.punchline: Implied: Tony gets beaten up instead (the '[14:40] What is this?' reaction suggests the fight went badly for Tony). The 'now who did you say the jerk was, jerk?' is a pre-victory boast that sets up an implied slapstick reversal
jokes.explanation: Setup for a physical reversal. The line itself is a decent pre-fight boast but the payoff is implied/visual. Relies on physical comedy we can't see in the transcript.

jokes.text: What does that sign say? / No bare feet. / What does that sign say? / No fighting. / What does it mean? / No fighting. / You owe me one gumball machine!
jokes.setup: Lou catches the boys fighting and delivers a Socratic lesson about the rules
jokes.punchline: After the grave civics lesson about rules, Lou's immediate demand is 'You owe me one gumball machine!' — the sign-based moral authority dissolves instantly into personal grievance
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — the Socratic sign-reading builds expectation of a principled lecture, then Lou deflates it with his petty personal property grievance. The gumball machine is a perfect specific detail. Character comedy working well.

jokes.text: Carl Lipbaum died last week in summer school from a severe anxiety attack. / I heard he swallowed his vomit during a test.
jokes.setup: Lou makes a somber announcement about a caddy's death
jokes.punchline: A caddy interjects with the specific, medically graphic cause — 'swallowed his vomit during a test' — delivered as simple information-sharing
jokes.explanation: The tonally inappropriate specificity of the vomit death information delivered in a solemn announcement context is good dark comedy. The deadpan delivery and the visual of a caddy helpfully providing medical details mid-eulogy is funny.

jokes.text: He was a brown nose, Lou! You hated him. / Shut up! That means the caddy scholarship is available again.
jokes.setup: Lou calls Lipbaum 'a good caddy and a good kid' in his eulogy
jokes.punchline: A caddy cuts through the sanctimony — 'He was a brown nose, Lou! You hated him!' — exposing the eulogy as pure performance; Lou's response ('Shut up!') confirms it
jokes.explanation: Nicely deflates the pompous mini-eulogy. The caddy's interruption is the kind of truth-to-power moment that gets a solid laugh, and Lou's 'Shut up!' confirmation is perfect.

jokes.text: And anyone who's interested should go see Judge Smails. / And kiss his ass!
jokes.setup: Lou announces the caddy scholarship is available and tells the caddies to see Judge Smails
jokes.punchline: A caddy adds 'And kiss his ass!' as the implied prerequisite for getting the scholarship
jokes.explanation: Good setup/punchline with the institutional corruption punchline landing as a rude but accurate commentary on how patronage works. Lou's 'That would help' is a great bonus beat.

jokes.text: You! Angie! Pick up that blood.
jokes.setup: Lou concludes his caddy briefing and starts sending people off
jokes.punchline: 'Pick up that blood' — delivered as a totally routine cleanup instruction, suggesting blood on the ground is a mundane occupational hazard at Bushwood
jokes.explanation: Brilliant throwaway. The casualness of 'Pick up that blood' — four words, as routine as 'pick up those cups' — is superb dark comedy. It implies a world where caddy violence is so common that blood cleanup is just part of the job description. One of the best single lines in this section.

jokes.text: Just snake a tube down her nose and I'll be there in four or five hours.
jokes.setup: Dr. Beeper is paged on the golf course and delegates a medical situation to cover his tee time
jokes.punchline: His medical instruction — 'snake a tube down her nose' — delivered while focused on golf, with the casual timeline of 'four or five hours' for what sounds like an urgent medical situation
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy establishing Dr. Beeper's character — his golf game takes absolute priority over patient care. 'Four or five hours' is the right number; too precise would kill it, too vague would soften it. The casual brutality of the medical instruction is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: Look at the wax build-up on those shoes! This is fine leather! I want that wax stripped off and I want them creamed and buffed with a fine chamois and I want them now! Chop-chop!
jokes.setup: Judge Smails arrives at the club and immediately issues grandiose demands about his shoes
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity of shoe-care instructions — strip, cream, buff, chamois — delivered with the urgency of a military commander, culminating in 'Chop-chop!', is a perfect character portrait of petty tyranny
jokes.explanation: Excellent character establishment for Judge Smails — the shoe-care tantrum shows his combination of elitism, pomposity, and petty authority in one compact scene. 'Chop-chop!' is a great period-specific power-word that dates his entitlement perfectly.

jokes.text: Spaulding! Get dressed. You're playing golf today. / No, I'm not, Grandpa! I'm playing tennis! / You're playing golf and you're going to like it! / What about my asthma? / I'll give you asthma!
jokes.setup: Judge Smails conscripts his grandson Spaulding into golf despite Spaulding's protests
jokes.punchline: 'I'll give you asthma!' — a threat that makes no logical sense (you can't give someone asthma) but perfectly captures the Judge's authoritarian fury and willingness to threaten anything
jokes.explanation: One of the best Smails lines in the reel. 'I'll give you asthma!' works because it's a physically impossible threat delivered with absolute conviction. The Judge is so autocratic he threatens to give a child a respiratory illness. The illogic IS the joke. High quotability.

jokes.text: Oh, I don't keep score, Judge. / How do you measure yourself with other golfers? / By height.
jokes.setup: Judge Smails asks Ty Webb what he shot today, implying competitive comparison is the point of golf
jokes.punchline: 'By height.' — Ty rejects the entire competitive framework of golf and replaces it with a measurement metric so irrelevant it loops back to being philosophical
jokes.explanation: One of the two or three best jokes in the reel. The setup is a completely normal golf question; Ty's first answer ('I don't keep score') is already a good character beat; but the follow-up — 'By height' — is a genuinely surprising, perfectly economical punchline that demolishes competitive ego in two words. It could only come from Ty Webb. The joke has perfect structure, extraordinary economy, and maximum character integration. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably surpasses it.

jokes.text: Don't sell yourself short, Judge. You're a tremendous slouch.
jokes.setup: Judge Smails is boasting about his golf game and says 'I'm no slouch, myself'
jokes.punchline: 'Don't sell yourself short, Judge. You're a tremendous slouch.' — Ty agrees with the Judge while completely reversing the intended compliment, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Among the best-crafted jokes in the reel. The structure is elegant: Smails's self-deprecating boast ('I'm no slouch') contains an opening, and Ty weaponizes the exact word the Judge used. 'You're a tremendous slouch' is a perfect inversion — he takes the Judge's own self-minimizing language and maximizes it into an insult. The word 'tremendous' elevating 'slouch' is the killer detail. Deadpan delivery is essential. High-craft, high-impact, highly quotable.

jokes.text: Have you heard the latest one about the Jew, the Catholic and the colored boy who went to heaven? / That's a doozie, Judge! / Colored boy? / Why, you son of a bitch! I'll fix you!
jokes.setup: Judge Smails launches into what appears to be a bigoted joke; Czervik reacts to 'colored boy'
jokes.punchline: Before Smails can even finish the setup of his joke, Czervik reacts with pointed offense to 'colored boy' and Smails's response — 'You son of a bitch! I'll fix you!' — reveals more about Smails's character than the actual joke would have
jokes.explanation: Smart structure — the punchline is not the joke but the reaction, and what it reveals. Smails is established as a bigot AND as someone who responds to being called out with explosive entitled fury. 'That's a doozie, Judge!' (probably from a sycophant) adds a layer. The joke does real character work without being merely shock-dependent.

jokes.text: Here you are, kid. Park my car. Get my bags. And put on some weight, will you?
jokes.setup: Al Czervik arrives at the club and immediately issues orders to a caddy
jokes.punchline: After the standard imperious arrival instructions, he adds 'And put on some weight, will you?' — a completely irrelevant personal remark delivered as if it's the most practical of his requests
jokes.explanation: Good Czervik arrival joke — he delivers the standard rich-guy valet routine then appends a completely personal, unrequested physical instruction as a matter of course. Establishes Czervik's particular brand of boorish obliviousness.

jokes.text: Hey, Wang! What's with the pictures? It's a parking lot! Come on.
jokes.setup: Czervik's guest Mr. Wang is apparently taking photos of the parking lot
jokes.punchline: Czervik calls this out with 'What's with the pictures? It's a parking lot!' — the joke playing on the stereotype of Asian tourists photographing mundane Americana, delivered by Czervik without any self-awareness
jokes.explanation: One of the weaker jokes in the reel. The humor relies on a dated ethnic stereotype (Asian tourist with camera) with no real twist or subversion. Czervik's obliviousness is in character but the base material is a cliché. Low earned_vs_cheap score.

jokes.text: I think this place is restricted, so don't tell them you're Jewish, okay?
jokes.setup: Czervik arrives at Bushwood Country Club with his guest Mr. Wang
jokes.punchline: Czervik, clearly Jewish himself, warns Wang not to reveal he's Jewish — a joke that (1) confirms the club IS restricted/antisemitic, (2) reveals Czervik has gotten in despite this, and (3) is delivered as friendly practical advice rather than outrage
jokes.explanation: Sharp social satire in one line. The joke does several things: confirms Bushwood's antisemitism as an open secret, characterizes Czervik as someone who works around institutional bigotry rather than confronting it, and has a kind of resigned pragmatic humor. Czervik telling Wang (presumably not Jewish) not to 'tell them he's Jewish' is also funny as an absurd misdirection — why would Wang be suspected?

jokes.text: I think this place is restricted, so don't tell them you're Jewish, okay?
jokes.setup: Al is arriving at an obviously exclusionary country club
jokes.punchline: He casually tells his guest not to reveal being Jewish — the club's antisemitism is matter-of-factly noted by the man who is about to run roughshod over the entire establishment
jokes.explanation: Sharp social satire compressed into one sentence. The joke works because Czervik delivers it without outrage — it's a practical tip, not a complaint. The casualness is the point: this is just how things are, and Czervik is about to blow the whole thing up anyway.

jokes.text: This is the worst-looking hat I ever saw! You buy a hat like this, I'll bet you get a free bowl of soup, huh? / Oh, it looks good on you, though.
jokes.setup: Czervik notices someone's hat while shopping in the pro shop
jokes.punchline: He delivers a devastating 'free bowl of soup' insult, then immediately softens it with 'Oh, it looks good on you, though' — a classic Rodney Dangerfield machine-gun comedy structure: insult-then-compliment-reversal
jokes.explanation: Classic Rodney Dangerfield. The joke has two beats: the soup insult (which is an excellent specific image — 'free bowl of soup' perfectly conjures the hat's cheapness) and then the immediate pivot to 'it looks good on you, though' as a simultaneously hollow consolation and additional insult. The structure is tight, the image is vivid, and the delivery timing is everything. Among the most quotable lines in the film. The hat-and-soup image has become iconic.

jokes.text: Who wants it, huh? / I'll take Smails if nobody wants him. / Brown nose!
jokes.setup: Lou is assigning caddies to golfers, including Judge Smails
jokes.punchline: A caddy volunteers for Smails 'if nobody wants him' — implying Smails is an undesirable client — and Lou immediately calls them a brown nose for it
jokes.explanation: Good beat that plays on both the scholarship subtext (volunteering for Smails = courting his favor) and Lou's contempt for sycophancy, despite having just confirmed ass-kissing works. Character consistent.

jokes.text: Madonna with meatballs!
jokes.setup: Spaulding reacts to something (presumably a bad shot or an unexpected sight) on the golf course
jokes.punchline: 'Madonna with meatballs!' — an entirely original, context-free profanity substitute that is both deeply specific (Italian-American cultural reference) and completely nonsensical as an expletive
jokes.explanation: Genuinely inventive. 'Madonna with meatballs!' as an exclamation is funny precisely because of its specificity — it's not random, it has an internal cultural logic, but it makes no sense as an expression of frustration. Spaulding's invented profanity is a great character detail for a privileged kid who can't swear in front of his grandfather.

jokes.text: Turds! / Spaulding! How many times have I spoken to you about your language? / Sorry, Grandpa. I forgot.
jokes.setup: Spaulding has been using inventive substitute profanity; now he drops a plain 'Turds!'
jokes.punchline: Judge Smails reprimands him gravely, as if 'Turds' is a serious language violation — implying Smails genuinely polices his grandson's speech while Spaulding continues to find workarounds
jokes.explanation: Running gag payoff for the Spaulding profanity bit. 'Turds' after 'Madonna with meatballs' is a funny downgrade — having been careful to invent surrogates, he eventually just says 'Turds.' Good character consistency.

jokes.text: It must be a nice change from dreary old Manhattan. / Yes. I was getting really tired of having fun all the time.
jokes.setup: Judge Smails condescendingly implies that Bushwood Country Club is a fun place for Lacey versus 'dreary old Manhattan'
jokes.punchline: Lacey's deadpan reversal — 'Yes. I was getting really tired of having fun all the time.' — is the perfect young sophisticate's dismissal of the Judge's provincial smugness
jokes.explanation: Lacey Underall's introduction is immediately strong. The joke is a perfect deadpan reversal — she takes Smails's condescension and flips it into a dismissal of everything he thinks is appealing about Bushwood. 'Really tired of having fun all the time' is a great line because it's simultaneously true (she sounds jaded) and a perfect put-down of Smails's delusion. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in structure and economy.

jokes.text: Double turds!
jokes.setup: Spaulding has been reprimanded for saying 'Turds'; he sees something new that upsets him
jokes.punchline: 'Double turds!' — escalating his profanity with 'Double' as a multiplier, suggesting he has an internal rating system for profanity based on severity of situation
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the running gag. 'Double turds!' works because it confirms Spaulding has a whole taxonomy — single turd, double turd — implying a severity scale. The addition of 'Double' is both childish and logical in its own internal system. Good rewatch bonus as the gag payoff.

jokes.text: Hey, Whitey! Where's your hat?
jokes.setup: Czervik is on the first tee, encountering Judge Smails's group
jokes.punchline: Czervik calls Judge Smails 'Whitey' — an aggressive, oblivious, or deliberately provocative nickname — with the follow-up about the hat implying Smails looks like he should have a hat (possibly a callback to the hat joke, or simply Czervik being immediately brash)
jokes.explanation: Good Czervik entrance to Smails's world — immediately nicknames him, immediately asks an odd question. Establishes the antagonistic dynamic with Smails and sets up the film's central class conflict. 'Whitey' is a good choice of nickname because it's both a physical description and an ethnic/class signifier that Smails would find infuriating.

jokes.text: I bet you slice it into the woods. A hundred bucks! / Gambling is illegal at Bushwood, sir, and I never slice!
jokes.setup: Czervik heckles Smails on the tee, betting he'll slice. Smails pompously declares gambling illegal AND that he never slices.
jokes.punchline: He immediately slices it into the woods (implied by 'Damn!' at 21:03), making both declarations wrong simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup: Smails doubles down with a pompous denial, and reality immediately proves him wrong on both counts. The structure is tight — setup, overconfident denial, instant comeuppance. Character integration is strong because Smails's self-important bluster is his defining trait. Works beautifully on rewatch because you anticipate the slice.

jokes.text: Damn! / Okay! You can owe me! / I owe you nothing!
jokes.setup: Smails has just sliced despite declaring he never slices and that gambling is illegal.
jokes.punchline: Czervik pivots to collecting the illegal bet; Smails refuses to honor the bet he said was illegal — meaning he only invoked the rule to avoid losing, not from principle.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to joke #1. 'I owe you nothing!' is a perfect character beat — Smails only cited the gambling rule as a shield, and when it suits him he abandons it. Very economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: You want your driver? / No, he's not my type. / Hey, that's a joke! I'm kidding. Give me the driver.
jokes.setup: Danny offers the Judge his driver (the golf club). Smails misreads the offer as offering him a chauffeur.
jokes.punchline: Smails makes an unexpected queer-panic non-joke ('not my type') about the chauffeur, then immediately breaks the tension by explaining it's a joke — which itself is funny because he's so desperate for the caddy to find him charming.
jokes.explanation: A mild wordplay joke elevated by Smails breaking his own joke immediately — 'That's a joke! I'm kidding!' shows him craving approval from the caddy he looks down on. Functional but not memorable.

jokes.text: Don't count that! I was interfered with.
jokes.setup: Smails has apparently hit a terrible shot in front of his group.
jokes.punchline: He immediately refuses to count it, claiming interference — the classic bad golfer's excuse delivered with total authority.
jokes.explanation: Economy is excellent — four words do all the work. The joke is very character-specific to Smails's combination of incompetence and unearned authority. Not original in concept (the cheating golfer is a classic) but executed crispy.

jokes.text: By the way, what did Mr. Webb shoot this morning? / Oh, he doesn't keep score, sir. / I know, but just guess. Eighty? Seventy-five? / More like 68, I think.
jokes.setup: Smails fishes for intel on a rival golfer, suggesting numbers like 80 or 75 (bad scores) as his 'guess.'
jokes.punchline: Danny deadpans '68' — far better than Smails hoped — deflating the Judge's ego completely.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Smails's leading questions — he wants validation and Danny innocently torpedoes it. Good character work; Smails's insecurity about his golf game is well-mined here.

jokes.text: Why don't you improve your lie a little, sir? / Yes, yes. Winter rules.
jokes.setup: Smails has a bad lie. Danny (the caddy who needs a favor) gently suggests cheating.
jokes.punchline: Smails immediately invokes 'winter rules' — a real but misapplied golf rule used as cover for cheating — with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the complicity — caddy enables the cheating judge. 'Winter rules' is insider golf humor that lands well with the audience Caddyshack is pitched at. Solid but minor.

jokes.text: I should have yelled two!
jokes.setup: Smails has just hit a wayward shot and presumably yelled 'Fore!' Standard golf warning.
jokes.punchline: 'I should have yelled two!' — implying the shot only traveled two yards, not four. A self-deprecating golf pun.
jokes.explanation: A compact, clever wordplay joke on the golf term 'fore' (four) vs. the distance traveled (two). Economical and genuinely witty. Smails self-deprecating is slightly surprising, adding a touch of character complexity.

jokes.text: What have you got in here, rocks? / When I was your age, I would lug 50 pounds of ice up five, six flights of stairs!
jokes.setup: Smails complains the golf bag is heavy, expecting sympathy.
jokes.punchline: Danny (the caddy, who is supposed to carry the bag) responds with a 'back in my day' boast about lugging 50 lbs of ice up six flights — a completely irrelevant flex that refuses to concede the point.
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the total irrelevance of the ice-hauling boast — Danny refuses to validate Smails's complaint and instead redirects to a macho non-sequitur. It's character-specific to Danny's braggadocio and the class dynamic at play.

jokes.text: So what? / So let's dance!
jokes.setup: Danny has told a story about lugging ice. Smails asks 'so what?' expecting a point.
jokes.punchline: 'So let's dance!' — an utterly non-sequitur response that escalates the absurdity and suggests Danny is spoiling for a confrontation using the strangest possible pivot.
jokes.explanation: Three words do enormous work. The pivot from blue-collar pride to a dance challenge is delightfully absurd and very Caddyshack in its anarchic energy. Economy score is nearly perfect — there's no fat here at all.

jokes.text: Music is a violation of our personal privacy! He is breaking the law!
jokes.setup: Al Czervik is blasting music from his golf bag. Smails is outraged.
jokes.punchline: Smails invokes 'the law' over someone playing music on a golf course — pompous overreach that reveals his authoritarian character.
jokes.explanation: Functional Smails character comedy — his hair-trigger legal threats are consistent with his character. Not a memorable line but adds to the portrait of pomposity.

jokes.text: I planned to go to law school after I graduated, but it looks like my folks won't have enough money to put me through college. / Well, the world needs ditchdiggers, too.
jokes.setup: Danny sincerely shares his aspirations and financial hardship with the Judge — a moment of genuine vulnerability from a kid seeking the scholarship.
jokes.punchline: Smails, the man who controls Danny's scholarship fate, responds with 'Well, the world needs ditchdiggers, too' — a casually cruel class-based dismissal delivered without malice, which makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest lines in this reel. It's become a cultural touchstone for clueless elitism. The joke earns its impact because it arrives in a moment of genuine pathos — Danny is sincere, the cruelty is inadvertent, which makes it funnier and darker simultaneously. 'The world needs ditchdiggers, too' is utterly Smails — it couldn't be delivered by any other character. Quotability is near-perfect; people still use this line. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Great big gobs of greasy grimy gopher guts.
jokes.setup: Carl is alone, narrating his war on gophers, in full psychological breakdown mode.
jokes.punchline: He launches into a children's playground chant ('great big gobs of greasy grimy gopher guts') as psychological warfare against the gophers — the incongruity of a grown man using nursery rhyme logic as military strategy.
jokes.explanation: Bill Murray's total commitment to Carl's delusional logic is what makes this land. The chant itself is childhood absurdity; in the mouth of a grown man threatening gophers it becomes deeply funny. Character-specific — no one but Carl.

jokes.text: How about a nice, cool drink, varmints? Scum, slime. Menace to the golfing industry!
jokes.setup: Carl is apparently offering the gophers a drink — playing both good cop and bad cop with himself.
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots from benevolent host ('nice, cool drink') to unhinged aggressor ('Scum, slime. Menace to the golfing industry!') in one breath.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from hospitality to hostility in a single breath is very Bill Murray — this reads as largely improvised and captures Carl's fractured psychology perfectly. 'Menace to the golfing industry' as an epithet for gophers is an inspired absurd escalation.

jokes.text: You know you're a disgrace. You're varmints. You're one of the lowest members of the food chain and you'll probably be replaced by the rat.
jokes.setup: Carl is lecturing gophers on their place in the natural order.
jokes.punchline: The evolutionary insult — 'you'll probably be replaced by the rat' — delivered with genuine contempt as if the gophers can hear and be wounded by this.
jokes.explanation: Carl's earnest moralizing at animals is a rich comedic vein. The specific evolutionary put-down ('replaced by the rat') shows an unexpected faux-intellectual logic that's very characteristic of Murray's improvised Carl material.

jokes.text: Come to Carl, varmint.
jokes.setup: Carl has worked himself into a full tactical monologue about flooding the gopher tunnels.
jokes.punchline: He ends with the intimate, almost tender 'Come to Carl, varmint' — a psychotic lullaby that collapses the distance between hunter and prey.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. The intimacy of 'Come to Carl' after all the aggression is a tonal reversal that is pitch-perfect. It's deeply character-specific — only Carl's fractured tenderness makes this work. Economy is nearly flawless. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Okay! I guess we're playing for keeps now. I guess the kidding around is pretty much over, huh? I guess it's just a matter now of pumping about 15,000 gallons of water down there to teach you a little bit of a lesson. Is that it? I think it is!
jokes.setup: Carl has decided to flood the gopher tunnels as his tactical solution.
jokes.punchline: The escalating self-narration — 'I guess... I guess... I guess...' — builds to '15,000 gallons of water' as a 'lesson,' the disproportionality of the response treated as perfectly reasonable.
jokes.explanation: Murray's escalating faux-casual self-narration is very strong here. '15,000 gallons of water to teach you a lesson' frames aquatic mass destruction as a pedagogical tool, which is classic Carl. A bit long, hence the economy dip.

jokes.text: They say for Italians this is skilled labor, you know that? / No, actually, I'm a rich millionaire. You see, my doctor told me to get out and carry golf bags a couple of times a week. / Oh, you're a funny kid. What time are you due back in Boys Town?
jokes.setup: Czervik makes an ethnic crack about Italians doing caddy work. Danny (or another caddy) fires back with a deadpan reversal — he's actually a millionaire doing this for health reasons.
jokes.punchline: Czervik, unable to be one-upped, retorts with 'What time are you due back in Boys Town?' — a sharp class-based insult that reasserts his dominance while acknowledging the kid got him.
jokes.explanation: A sharp volley exchange. The ethnic crack is period-specific in its edge; the deadpan reversal is well-constructed; and 'Boys Town' as a comeback shows Czervik pivoting quickly. The whole exchange has the rhythm of a good joke battle.

jokes.text: Albert Einstein gave me this. Nice man. He made a fortune in physics.
jokes.setup: Czervik is showing off some possession (likely his elaborate golf bag or equipment) and name-drops Einstein.
jokes.punchline: 'He made a fortune in physics' — a category error that treats physics as a wealth-generating profession like real estate, revealing Czervik's pure money-brain worldview.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent. 'He made a fortune in physics' is a perfectly constructed character joke — it's impossible unless delivered by someone whose only metric of achievement is money. The deadpan delivery of a logical impossibility as obvious fact is Dangerfield at his best. Originality is high — the specific category error is fresh and precise. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: My main satisfaction is working with young people like yourself at our new Youtheran Center.
jokes.setup: Smails is positioning himself as a benefactor of youth — a contrast with his actual contempt for young people (see: 'ditchdiggers').
jokes.punchline: The gap between Smails's self-image (generous mentor) and his behavior (dismissive, cruel) is the ongoing ironic joke. 'Youtheran' also sounds like 'Lutheran' mashed with 'youth,' a possible malapropism gag.
jokes.explanation: Minor ironic character moment — the 'Youtheran' mash-up may be intentional wordplay, and the hypocrisy irony is consistent. But it's a soft joke, dependent on context more than craft.

jokes.text: I've often thought of entering the priesthood. / Oh, are you Roman Catholic? / I'm sorry, but I'm afraid you can't come.
jokes.setup: Danny mentions considering the priesthood as a vocation. Smails asks if he's Catholic — implying a Protestant/WASP club's bias.
jokes.punchline: Smails refuses to invite Danny to the 'Youtheran Center' because he's apparently Catholic — casual sectarian discrimination played entirely straight.
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed. Smails asks a leading question that feels like inclusion, then uses the answer to exclude. The bigotry is so matter-of-fact it becomes darkly funny. Deepens the class/status comedy that runs through the film.

jokes.text: Not bad, huh? And I'll have 2,000 more units in the next two years! I bet they'd love a great shopping mall right here! Condos over there! Plenty of parking. I tell you, country clubs and cemeteries are the biggest wasters of prime real estate! Dead people? They don't want to be buried nowadays. Ecology, right?
jokes.setup: Czervik is surveying the golf course and pitching his development vision to anyone nearby.
jokes.punchline: 'Dead people? They don't want to be buried nowadays. Ecology, right?' — the logical absurdity of speaking for the preferences of the dead while desecrating the sanctity of a cemetery, presented as environmental concern.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dangerfield/Czervik: the gleeful philistinism of turning sacred space into parking lots. 'Dead people don't want to be buried — ecology, right?' is a perfectly absurd construction where he co-opts environmental language to justify greed. High character integration.

jokes.text: Ask Wang. He'll tell you. We just bought property behind the Great Wall. On the good side!
jokes.setup: Czervik is continuing to brag about his real estate empire.
jokes.punchline: 'On the good side!' — implies there is a good side of the Great Wall of China, and that Czervik has figured out which one it is, as if the entire structure is just a geographic feature affecting property values.
jokes.explanation: The Great Wall reduced to a neighborhood amenity is a great Czervik joke. 'The good side' is the killer phrase — it treats one of the world's great monuments the way a realtor talks about being 'on the right side of the tracks.'

jokes.text: I want a hamburger. / No, a cheeseburger. / I want a hot dog. / I want a milkshake. / You'll get nothing and like it!
jokes.setup: Children (or family members) place increasingly demanding food orders at the club.
jokes.punchline: Smails snaps 'You'll get nothing and like it!' — the definitive authoritarian non-answer to a food order, which also reveals his stinginess despite being a Judge and club member.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. The escalating food requests (hamburger → cheeseburger → hot dog → milkshake) build the perfect rhythm for Smails's nuclear response. The line has entered common usage precisely because it encapsulates a certain type of tyrannical cheapness. Economy is perfect. Character integration is very high — Smails's pompous authoritarianism being applied to a child's snack order is exactly right. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Are you going out with me tonight, Maggie? / Yes. To my room? / I've got to work in the dining room tonight. / Come work with me. You can bus tables. / I've never done that. / It's easy. You fill the water glass, replace the butter... If they drop a fork, you give them another one. / I don't think I can handle that.
jokes.setup: Danny is trying to get Maggie to come to his room; she redirects with her work obligations.
jokes.punchline: Danny explains busing tables — a job so simple a child could do it — with earnest detail, and Maggie responds 'I don't think I can handle that,' which works as (a) genuine airheadedness or (b) deflection to avoid Danny's room.
jokes.explanation: Mild comedy of incompetence. The joke is Maggie claiming she can't handle the most elementary restaurant task. It's functional but a little underwritten — the comedic potential of this exchange isn't fully exploited.

jokes.text: License to kill gophers by the government of the United Nations. Man... free to kill gophers at will. To kill, you must know your enemy. In this case, my enemy is a varmint, and a varmint will never quit. Ever! They're like the Viet Cong. Varmint Cong!
jokes.setup: Carl is continuing his gopher war monologue, now invoking geopolitical authority.
jokes.punchline: 'Varmint Cong!' — the moment Carl's military obsession crystallizes into the perfect mashup portmanteau, treating golf course rodents as a guerrilla insurgency.
jokes.explanation: The 'Varmint Cong' coinage is excellent — it's the natural endpoint of Carl's Vietnam-vet-turned-groundskeeper delusion. The escalation from 'UN license to kill gophers' through the military doctrine monologue to this invented compound word is well-structured. It's a word that couldn't exist outside this character. Originality and character integration are both exceptional. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: And that's all she wrote.
jokes.setup: Carl has laid out his entire tactical military doctrine for fighting gophers.
jokes.punchline: He punctuates the insane monologue with the most banal, matter-of-fact sign-off possible — 'And that's all she wrote' — as if he's just explained a sensible business plan.
jokes.explanation: The deflation gag — after a soaring absurd rant, the most commonplace exit line. Works through contrast and economy. Character-specific to Carl's earnest obliviousness.

jokes.text: Are you going to eat your fat? / You're looking lovely this evening, Mrs. Smails.
jokes.setup: Czervik has apparently just said something rude to Mrs. Smails (asking about her fat), then immediately pivots to a compliment.
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of 'are you going to eat your fat?' directly followed by 'you're looking lovely' — Czervik's social obliviousness operating at peak velocity.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dangerfield social obliviousness. The pivot from insulting to complimentary without any awareness that the insult still hangs in the air is very well timed. Czervik's charm offensive that's really just an offense.

jokes.text: They invented the game there, except they call it 'gof'... without the 'L' as we do.
jokes.setup: Smails is explaining the Scottish origins of golf to someone at the dinner table, displaying his expertise.
jokes.punchline: 'Except they call it gof — without the L as we do' — Smails, in trying to prove his sophistication, says something that's either completely wrong or nonsensical, delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Smails's false expertise — he invents or misremembers etymology and presents it authoritatively. The specific non-sequitur 'without the L as we do' is a good piece of absurdist character writing.

jokes.text: Hey, doll, could you scare up another round for our table? And tell the cook this is low-grade dog food. Here, take this for yourself. Gee, I had better food at the ballgame! I tell you, this steak still has marks where the jockey was hitting it.
jokes.setup: Czervik is at dinner at the upscale club, treating the waitress and the food with his characteristic contempt.
jokes.punchline: 'This steak still has marks where the jockey was hitting it' — a classic Dangerfield racetrack-based food insult implying the steak came from a racehorse.
jokes.explanation: The jockey/steak joke is a great Dangerfield construction — the visual of whip marks on the meat is specific and vivid. The setup through 'low-grade dog food' and the ballgame comparison builds to the punchline well. Pure Dangerfield rhythm.

jokes.text: Oh, did somebody step on a duck?
jokes.setup: Someone at the table (implied: Mrs. Smails or another dignified club member) has passed gas audibly.
jokes.punchline: Czervik's response — 'did somebody step on a duck?' — is a classic euphemism for a fart, delivered in this upscale dining room with perfect timing.
jokes.explanation: One of the best-known lines from the film. The fart joke is lowbrow but the phrasing — 'step on a duck' — is an elegant euphemism. Context matters enormously: a formal country club dinner is the perfect setting for this. It's not the joke that's great, it's the timing and the setting doing the heavy lifting. Economy is perfect.

jokes.text: Oh, the graveyard is two blocks to the left, okay?
jokes.setup: Someone older (possibly Smails or a club elder) has made a comment that invites the riff.
jokes.punchline: Czervik directs them to the graveyard — the implication being they're old enough to be dead. A casual death joke delivered to someone's face at the dinner table.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dangerfield dark-age-joke rhythm. It's not his most original construction but it lands in context because of the upscale setting and Czervik's total lack of filter.

jokes.text: Hey, waiter, here. This is for you, all right? Oh! Captain Hook! / Oh, how about the grand you owe me, huh? / Aw, forget about it. I'm just kidding.
jokes.setup: Czervik tips the waiter conspicuously and then pivots to remind Smails of a debt.
jokes.punchline: He calls Smails 'Captain Hook' (presumably targeting his personality or appearance), then brings up the money owed, then immediately waves it away — using the debt as a power move while pretending to be magnanimous.
jokes.explanation: Good character work for Czervik — the performative generosity covering the aggressive debt reminder. 'Captain Hook' as a nickname for Smails is sharp.

jokes.text: Oh, how about the grand you owe me, huh? Aw, forget about it. I'm just kidding.
jokes.setup: Al spots someone who owes him money at the party
jokes.punchline: He raises it publicly, humiliating the person, then immediately waves it off — the false graciousness is the insult
jokes.explanation: A quick social embarrassment joke. The pattern (call someone out → immediately pretend it's a joke) is a Dangerfield rhythm staple. Functional.

jokes.text: Hey, you must have been something before electricity, huh?
jokes.setup: Czervik is talking to Smails's wife (an older, formal woman).
jokes.punchline: 'You must have been something before electricity' — implying she was attractive before she aged, with 'before electricity' as a measure of extreme age. A brutal age insult delivered as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: One of Dangerfield's best lines in the film. 'Before electricity' is an inspired measure of age — it's both a compliment (you were once something) and a devastating insult (you're pre-electric). The economy is superb — one sentence does everything. It couldn't come from anyone but Czervik. Genuinely quotable and original. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Hey, doll, how are you, huh? You live alone? / Hey, Rabbi, nice seeing you. Folks, how are you? / And this is your grandson, huh? Oh, wonderful boy! / Yeah, he's a good boy. / Now I know why tigers eat their young.
jokes.setup: Czervik is working the room, being gregarious with a Rabbi and his family, cooing over a boy being presented to him.
jokes.punchline: After being told the boy is 'a good boy,' Czervik delivers 'Now I know why tigers eat their young' — a savage dark-comedy non sequitur suggesting the boy is so insufferable it justifies infanticide.
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed — the setup of Czervik being apparently delightful makes the tiger infanticide line land harder. It's a dark-comedy pivot of the highest Dangerfield order. Economical and devastating. High quotability.

jokes.text: The dance of the living dead!
jokes.setup: Czervik observes the formal, stiff dancing at the club event.
jokes.punchline: He dubs it 'the dance of the living dead' — a perfect description of the WASP country club set moving rigidly on a dance floor.
jokes.explanation: Five words do it all. The visual of stiff WASP country club dancing being labeled 'living dead' is sharp and class-specific. Very economical.

jokes.text: I know why you came here tonight. / Why? / That girl. Listen, I'd put that idea right out of your mind. She's been plucked more times than the rose of Tralee. Biggest whore on Fifth Avenue, I'm told!
jokes.setup: Czervik notices Danny's interest in a woman at the party.
jokes.punchline: 'She's been plucked more times than the rose of Tralee' — an ornate, almost poetic slut-shaming metaphor delivered with absolute confidence and followed by 'Biggest whore on Fifth Avenue, I'm told' — a bizarrely specific piece of gossip.
jokes.explanation: The 'rose of Tralee' metaphor is genuinely well-crafted — it's the kind of ornate expression that only exists in the mouth of an older vulgarian. The escalation to 'Fifth Avenue' as a geographic precision point is funny. Dated in its attitudes but the craft is there.

jokes.text: Pay no attention to that bush moving around there by that tree. It's just a bush. Don't even look twice at it. Nothing to be alarmed about.
jokes.setup: Carl Spackler is apparently hiding in a bush or wearing a bush disguise near the party, stalking the gopher.
jokes.punchline: Czervik draws everyone's attention to the moving bush while earnestly telling them not to look at it — the classic Streisand effect joke, making the weird thing impossible to ignore by insisting it's nothing.
jokes.explanation: Very visual comedy that relies heavily on what the audience sees (a moving bush at a formal party). The escalating reassurances — 'just a bush, don't even look twice, nothing to be alarmed about' — work perfectly because each one draws MORE attention. Rewatch bonus for the visual.

jokes.text: This looks like it could be gravy.
jokes.setup: Carl, who has been crawling through the grounds and landscaping, apparently finds/tastes some unidentified liquid.
jokes.punchline: 'This looks like it could be gravy' — Carl's total equanimity about discovering an unknown brown liquid, expressed as a hopeful culinary assessment.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Murray/Carl improvised-feeling lines in the reel. Seven words create a complete comedic universe: Carl is crawling around near a formal party, finds something brown, and his only thought is optimistic ('could be gravy'). The 'could be' is crucial — it's not certainty, it's hopeful. Economy is near-perfect. Deeply character-specific. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: I smell varmint poontang, and the only good varmint poontang is dead varmint poontang... I think.
jokes.setup: Carl is in full predator mode, tracking the gopher through the party grounds.
jokes.punchline: He adapts the 'only good [enemy] is a dead [enemy]' Vietnam-era construction to gopher sexuality, then pauses on '...I think' — a moment of genuine uncertainty about his own extreme position.
jokes.explanation: The '...I think' at the end is what elevates this. It's pure Bill Murray — Carl is so deep in his military mindset that he applies it to gopher sexuality, but then has a flicker of doubt about whether dead varmint poontang is actually the goal. That pause of self-questioning at the end of such an extreme statement is comedy gold. Completely character-specific. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Al built our condo in Palm Beach. / I need a drink. Nice meeting you.
jokes.setup: Someone introduces Ty Webb to Al Czervik, clearly expecting Ty to be impressed or interested.
jokes.punchline: Ty's immediate response to being told this real estate credential is 'I need a drink. Nice meeting you' — a dismissal so swift it's almost slapstick.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Ty Webb's Zen detachment — he has zero social obligation instincts. 'I need a drink. Nice meeting you' as a simultaneous greeting/farewell is very economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Hey! Can you make a bullshot? / Can you make a shoe smell?
jokes.setup: Czervik asks the bartender (or Ty) to make a bullshot (a cocktail).
jokes.punchline: Ty responds with 'Can you make a shoe smell?' — a nonsensical comeback that riffs on the word 'bull-shot' (bullshit + bull) with a shoe/smell absurdist mirror. It's either wordplay or pure Zen gibberish.
jokes.explanation: Very Ty Webb — the response is either a sharp non-sequitur or a subtle wordplay ('bullshot' / 'shoe smell' as parallel nonsense compounds) but either way it completely wrong-foots Czervik. Chevy Chase's Zen absurdism is well-deployed here.

jokes.text: What people here! Look at that one. The last time I saw a mouth like that, it had a hook in it!
jokes.setup: Czervik surveys the people at the party.
jokes.punchline: 'The last time I saw a mouth like that, it had a hook in it' — a fish insult comparing someone's large/strange mouth to a caught fish.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dangerfield construction — the unexpected comparative ('the last time I saw...') leading to a vivid specific image (hook in mouth). The fishing context is a nice country club thematic tie-in. Well-crafted insult comedy.

jokes.text: So what brings you to this nape of the woods... neck of the wape?
jokes.setup: Ty is talking to a woman at the party and attempts the idiom 'neck of the woods.'
jokes.punchline: He says 'nape of the woods' and then tries to correct to 'neck of the wape' — both wrong, in opposite directions, suggesting Ty's mind doesn't operate on normal idiom rails.
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed — Ty tries to self-correct but only makes it worse in a different direction ('neck of the wape'). It's not just a malapropism — it's a double malapropism that corrects the wrong word. This is sharp writing that also characterizes Ty as someone operating on a slightly different frequency. High character integration.

jokes.text: I'll bet you've got a lot of interesting stories about your ball landing in the road.
jokes.setup: Ty is talking to a pretty woman, ostensibly about golf.
jokes.punchline: The double entendre of 'ball landing in the road' as a golf reference that also sounds sexually suggestive — delivered with Ty's characteristic deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Mild double entendre in the Ty Webb flirtation register. Not his sharpest line — the innuendo is a bit obvious — but it maintains his character's oblique seduction style.

jokes.text: So what do you do? / I enjoy... skinny-skiing... / ...going to bullfights on acid.
jokes.setup: Lacey asks Ty the standard party question. He begins his list of hobbies.
jokes.punchline: 'Going to bullfights on acid' — an escalating absurd non-sequitur that pairs an extreme activity with an extreme substance, delivered completely deadpan as a normal hobby.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and perhaps in 1980s comedy. 'Going to bullfights on acid' is a perfect absurdist construction — it takes an already extreme activity (bullfights) and adds the modifier that makes it maximally unhinged, while Chevy Chase delivers it with the calm of someone saying 'I enjoy gardening.' Originality is exceptional — the specific combination is unforgettable. Character integration is near-perfect: only Ty Webb could say this. This is a genuine 8+ moment. Comparable to 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' in its compact, unforgettable absurdism.

jokes.text: I'll bet you've got a lot of nice ties.
jokes.setup: Following his absurdist hobbies, Ty seems to change tack entirely.
jokes.punchline: The completely banal and irrelevant observation about ties after talking about bullfights on acid — the deflation from extreme to mundane is the joke, plus it sets up the next joke.
jokes.explanation: The humor is almost entirely structural — the descent from 'bullfights on acid' to 'nice ties' is the comedy. Functions as a setup for the tie/Ty pun that follows, so its value increases in context.

jokes.text: What do you mean? / You want to tie me up with some of your ties... Ty?
jokes.setup: Ty says Lacey has nice ties. She asks what he means.
jokes.punchline: Lacey's comeback — 'You want to tie me up with some of your ties... Ty?' — a triple-play pun on 'tie' (neckwear), 'tie up' (bondage), and 'Ty' (his name), delivered as seduction.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever piece of wordplay that earns the callback. The triple meaning (ties/tie up/Ty) compressed into one sentence with a seductive delivery is sharp writing. The name pun at the end ('...Ty?') is the perfect capper.

jokes.text: Let's pretend... we're real human beings.
jokes.setup: Ty and Lacey are flirting at the party.
jokes.punchline: 'Let's pretend we're real human beings' — a line that acknowledges their mutual weirdness/artificiality while also being an absurdist non-sequitur seduction line.
jokes.explanation: Very strong. The existential absurdity of a flirtation line that questions the humanity of both parties is both funny and oddly poignant. It captures everything about Ty Webb — his detachment, his charm, his refusal to operate on normal social rails. 'Pretend we're real human beings' is a profound piece of deadpan that justifies 8+. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Who is that disgusting man over there? / I tell you, I never saw dead people smoke before!
jokes.setup: Someone asks about Czervik. His response or appearance provokes the 'dead people smoke' comment — either he's smoking in a gross way or someone is making an age/zombie joke about the people he's with.
jokes.punchline: 'I never saw dead people smoke before' — Czervik turning the insult back on the club members, characterizing them as corpses who smoke.
jokes.explanation: Good Czervik counter-volley — turning the 'disgusting' question back as a zombie observation on the club members. Consistent with his character's pattern of redirecting insults at the establishment.

jokes.text: Hey, you two should get a room, you know? Hey, Ringo, play something hot, will you? And you guys... take some more lessons!
jokes.setup: Czervik is walking through the party critiquing everything and everyone.
jokes.punchline: Telling the band's drummer 'Ringo' to play something hot, then telling the other musicians to take more lessons — commandeering the entire event's entertainment direction without being asked.
jokes.explanation: Calling the drummer 'Ringo' is a good pop-culture gag that shows Czervik's instant-nickname habit. 'Take some more lessons' as a drive-by insult is functional Dangerfield. Not his strongest material in this stretch.

jokes.text: Hey, Judge, give someone else a chance! You lucky devil! Come here, honey! And hey, loosen up! You're a lot of woman, you know?
jokes.setup: Czervik is dancing/interacting with women at the party, specifically targeting the Judge's social territory.
jokes.punchline: 'You're a lot of woman, you know?' — a backhanded compliment (possibly directed at a large or formidable woman) that Czervik delivers as pure flattery.
jokes.explanation: Functional Czervik chaos but not his best material. 'A lot of woman' is a standard Dangerfield-ism that works in context but isn't memorable on its own.

jokes.text: You want to make $14 the hard way? / You! You! You're no gentleman! / I'm no doorknob, either.
jokes.setup: Czervik propositions someone (possibly Mrs. Smails or another woman) with '$14 the hard way.' Smails is outraged and calls him 'no gentleman.'
jokes.punchline: Czervik's comeback — 'I'm no doorknob, either' — is a perfect non-sequitur that completely refuses to engage with the insult on its own terms. A doorknob has nothing to do with gentleman; it's pure deflection.
jokes.explanation: The '$14 the hard way' is a great vulgar hook, but 'I'm no doorknob, either' is the standout — it's a non-sequitur that works as a perfect non-answer. By refusing to defend against 'no gentleman' and instead denying being a doorknob, Czervik wins the exchange through pure absurdism. Very economical.

jokes.text: Wait up, girls. I've got a salami I've got to hide.
jokes.setup: Czervik is apparently trying to catch up with women leaving or moving away from him.
jokes.punchline: The double entendre of hiding a salami — both literally (he may actually have deli meat) and as a crude sexual reference — delivered as though a perfectly normal reason to follow women.
jokes.explanation: Classic Czervik innuendo. The ambiguity of whether it's literal (he actually has a salami — entirely possible given his character) makes it funnier than a straight double entendre. The 'Wait up, girls' as an urgent opening before such a weird reason is good rhythm.

jokes.text: I'll slack you off, you fuzzy little foreigner, and I'll fill your bagpipes with Wheatena!
jokes.setup: Smails is arguing with the groundskeeper or a club employee (possibly the man who suggested changing the holes), apparently a Scottish/foreign national with bagpipes.
jokes.punchline: 'I'll fill your bagpipes with Wheatena!' — Smails's threat involves filling bagpipes with a breakfast cereal brand, an absurdly specific and physically impractical threat that reveals his rage-fueled nonsense.
jokes.explanation: One of the most unexpected lines in this reel. 'Wheatena' (a hot cereal) in bagpipes is not a threat anyone has ever made — the specificity of the brand makes it extraordinary. Smails's blustering rage finding this precise absurdist outlet is sublime. The 'fuzzy little foreigner' setup gives the punchline perfect contrast. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Man in a boat overboard. / You beast! / You savage. / Come on, bark like a dog for me. / Bark like a dog! I will teach you the meaning of the word 'respect'!
jokes.setup: An altercation on or near Smails's boat. Someone ends up in the water or in distress.
jokes.punchline: Czervik demands Smails 'bark like a dog' as a dominance display, then threatens to 'teach him the meaning of respect' — an ironic inversion where the disrespectful one lectures on respect.
jokes.explanation: 'Bark like a dog for me' as a demand to a sitting judge is a great power-inversion moment. The irony of 'I will teach you the meaning of respect' coming from the most disrespectful character in the film is well-executed.

jokes.text: He decided to go to college instead. He went for four years. Did pretty well. At the end of his four years, the last semester, he was kicked out. You know what for? He was night-putting. Just putting at night... with the 15-year-old daughter of the Dean.
jokes.setup: Ty is telling Danny an inspirational story about a guy who gave up golf for college. The 'putting' metaphor builds, and 'night-putting' sounds like it might be a golf reference.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that 'night-putting with the dean's 15-year-old daughter' is not a golf metaphor at all — it's a statutory crime. The euphemism collapses into something much darker.
jokes.explanation: Very well structured misdirection — the inspirational-story format, the golf metaphor building, the pause before the reveal. The '15-year-old daughter of the Dean' lands as a dark non-sequitur. The structure is tight: setup as moral fable, payoff as crime confession. Would be even stronger if the age reveal weren't quite so dark, but the dissonance between format and content is exactly the joke.

jokes.text: You know who that guy was? / Take one good guess. / Bob Hope. / No, that guy was Mitch Cumstein, my roommate.
jokes.setup: Ty asks Danny to guess who the 'putting with the dean's daughter' guy was — dramatically building expectation of a famous name.
jokes.punchline: Danny guesses 'Bob Hope' (a reasonable famous-golfer guess). Ty deflates it entirely: 'No, that was Mitch Cumstein, my roommate' — nobody, an absolute nobody, with a slightly rude-sounding surname.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedic structure. The dramatic 'you know who that guy was?' — a classic setup for a famous-name reveal — is completely subverted by 'Mitch Cumstein, my roommate.' The deflation from 'Bob Hope' to an obscure roommate is perfectly calibrated. The name 'Cumstein' adds its own lowbrow bonus. This is a textbook misdirection/anticlimactic reveal executed at a high level. Justifies 8+ and is one of the reel's best jokes.

jokes.text: No, that guy was Mitch Cumstein, my roommate. He's a good guy. Don't be obsessed with your desires, Danny.
jokes.setup: Danny guessed Bob Hope; the expectation is that Ty will reveal it was himself.
jokes.punchline: It was neither Ty nor anyone famous — it was Mitch Cumstein, a completely unknown roommate, delivered as though the story was always going to be this mundane. The invented surname 'Cumstein' is itself a crude joke.
jokes.explanation: The triple misdirect is excellent: (1) we expected inspirational story, got dark scandal; (2) we expected Ty to be the protagonist; (3) we expected a famous person — it's Mitch Cumstein. The invented name 'Cumstein' containing a crude pun is an extra layer Ty either doesn't notice or finds normal. Followed by sage advice ('don't be obsessed with your desires') — wisdom from a story with no applicable lesson.

jokes.text: The Zen philosopher, Basho, once wrote, 'a flute with no holes is not a flute... and a doughnut with no hole is a Danish.'
jokes.setup: Ty is delivering profound philosophical wisdom to Danny after the Mitch Cumstein story.
jokes.punchline: The faux-Zen koan begins with genuine profundity ('a flute with no holes is not a flute') and pivots to 'a doughnut with no hole is a Danish' — which is both technically true and completely deflating as philosophy.
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in this reel and one of the best in the film. The structure is impeccable: establish the Zen register with a credible-sounding aphorism, then deliver a second clause that's both logically parallel AND completely banal.
