'A doughnut with no hole is a Danish' works on multiple levels: (1) it's technically accurate, (2) it maintains the grammatical structure of a koan, (3) it completely destroys the profundity. Chevy Chase's delivery ('He was a funny guy') as a capper is perfect. Originality is exceptional — this construction is completely unique to Ty Webb. This is a 9+ moment.

jokes.text: In one physical model of the universe, the shortest distance between two points is a straight line in the opposite direction.
jokes.setup: Ty and Danny are on the golf course. Ty is apparently giving golf/life advice.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a physics-esque statement ('shortest distance between two points is a straight line') and then appends 'in the opposite direction' — which is precisely wrong but delivered with total authority as an alternative cosmological model.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ty Webb absurdism — taking a well-known truth ('shortest distance is a straight line') and confidently contradicting it with 'in the opposite direction,' framed as an alternative physics model. It's not random nonsense; there's a precise intellectual structure to the wrong answer that makes it funnier. The 'one physical model' caveat adds academic legitimacy to the inversion. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Nice form. / Good luck, sucker.
jokes.setup: Ty has apparently just watched Danny practice or take a shot.
jokes.punchline: He compliments the form then immediately says 'Good luck, sucker' — genuine encouragement followed by a demolishing addendum that suggests the form doesn't matter.
jokes.explanation: Four words do the work. 'Good luck, sucker' as a send-off after mentorship is a perfect Ty Webb tonal switch. The 'sucker' makes it affectionately contemptuous — he means it fondly, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I'm christening my new sloop. What are you doing this Sunday? / No plans. / Great! How would you like to mow my lawn? I figured a college-bound fellow could use a few extra dollars.
jokes.setup: Smails builds up to what sounds like an invitation to a yacht club christening party.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is that he's inviting Danny to mow his lawn — not to the party. The 'college-bound fellow' framing makes the lawn-mowing offer sound like a scholarship.
jokes.explanation: Very strong structure — the misdirection of the party invitation pivoting to lawn service is a perfect Smails move. It's the 'ditchdiggers' joke in a different key: Smails always finds new ways to remind Danny of his place. The 'college-bound fellow could use a few extra dollars' rationale is especially cutting.

jokes.text: And... when you're finished... why don't you drop by the Yacht Club?
jokes.setup: After inviting Danny to mow his lawn, Smails adds the afterthought invitation to the Yacht Club.
jokes.punchline: The 'when you're finished' — meaning 'after you've done my lawn work' — reframes the social event as a reward for labor. Danny gets to attend the party only as a servant's bonus.
jokes.explanation: A good one-two with joke #61. The afterthought invitation structure perfectly captures Smails's class condescension — he invites Danny to the party only as an afterthought following labor. Well-integrated callback.

jokes.text: How about we go swimming? / I don't have the swimwear. Besides, I've never swum.
jokes.setup: Danny suggests swimming as a romantic move.
jokes.punchline: Maggie's excuse includes 'I've never swum' — a charmingly awkward grammatical construction (correct past participle, almost never used) that also reveals something about her character.
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. The humor is in 'I've never swum' as an oddly formal way to say you can't swim, combined with the swimwear excuse. Neither element is especially strong on its own.

jokes.text: I'll teach you. / Why don't you come on in and help me sort my holy cards first?
jokes.setup: Danny offers to teach Maggie to swim (a romantic gambit). She deflects with an alternative.
jokes.punchline: 'Why don't you come help me sort my holy cards first?' — Catholic devotional cards as a romantic distraction, implying she's both diverting Danny and perhaps using her faith as a chastity shield.
jokes.explanation: The Catholic detail adds texture — the same Catholicism that got Danny excluded from Smails's center is now being used by Maggie as an ersatz romantic deflection. 'Sort my holy cards' as a seduction-deflection is oddly specific and funny.

jokes.text: Hey, Bigfoot, don't trip in the water!
jokes.setup: Someone (likely a large caddy or worker) is near the water.
jokes.punchline: Calling them 'Bigfoot' and warning they don't trip — a standard large-person taunt in a country club setting.
jokes.explanation: Generic physical-appearance insult. 'Bigfoot' is a lazy taunt with no particular craft or character specificity. Below average for this film.

jokes.text: You put your suit on! / You shave your ass!
jokes.setup: Someone mocks another for making an effort to dress up (putting on a swimsuit).
jokes.punchline: 'You shave your ass!' — a crude, specific counter-insult that (a) implies the person commenting is hairy in a private area and (b) expresses disbelief at their criticism.
jokes.explanation: Crude but effective comeback. The specificity of 'shave your ass' as a retort is funnier than a generic insult — it implies intimate knowledge of the person's grooming habits. Works primarily through shock and bluntness.

jokes.text: Hi, Maggie. How was it? / How was what? / I guess it couldn't have been that great, then. / A lot you fucking know, D'Annunzio!
jokes.setup: D'Annunzio greets Maggie after her time with Danny, fishing for gossip about their sexual encounter.
jokes.punchline: Maggie's coy 'How was what?' prompts D'Annunzio's perfect deflating response ('couldn't have been that great then'), and her angry 'A lot you fucking know!' inadvertently confirms something did happen.
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured exchange. The logic chain is tight: (1) D'Annunzio's leading question, (2) Maggie's deflection, (3) D'Annunzio's perfect deflating inference ('I guess it couldn't have been that great'), (4) Maggie's angry denial that CONFIRMS something happened. The 'fucking' in 'A lot you fucking know' is the tell. The whole exchange is economical and dramatically ironic. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: She's incredible!
jokes.setup: Following the explosive Maggie/D'Annunzio exchange, Danny delivers his verdict.
jokes.punchline: 'She's incredible!' as a final button — Danny is in the dark about Maggie's anger at D'Annunzio, and his oblivious enthusiasm underscores the gap between his experience and the drama unfolding around him.
jokes.explanation: A good button — Danny's oblivious enthusiasm contrasting with the chaos just witnessed. Two words as an episode (reel) closer. The irony is that his 'incredible' refers to the sexual encounter while the audience has just watched Maggie deny it furiously.

jokes.text: She's incredible!
jokes.setup: Maggie has just angrily defended herself to D'Annunzio, confirming something happened with Danny
jokes.punchline: Danny's private, awestruck 'She's incredible!' — heard presumably as a reaction to her fire, not just the sex — delivered as a final button on the scene
jokes.explanation: A button on the scene — Danny's admiration serves as a capper that confirms the affair and adds a sweet ironic note. Economical but slight on its own.

jokes.text: I don't want to see another caddy body in this pool!
jokes.setup: Caddies have invaded the members' pool and need to be expelled — a standard authority-figure announcement
jokes.punchline: 'Another' caddy body implies this has happened before repeatedly, reducing the caddies to objects to be fished out rather than people
jokes.explanation: The word 'another' does enormous comedic work in a very short line — it implies a whole sordid institutional history of caddy pool invasions and reveals the club's dehumanizing attitude in a single word. Tight, character-specific, and lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Doodie!
jokes.setup: Pool is being cleared of caddies; official is in authority-figure mode issuing commands
jokes.punchline: The dignified command sequence ('Take your hands off her… put your clothes on… Out!') is suddenly interrupted by the discovery of a floating piece of excrement in the pool
jokes.explanation: The single-word scream after a rising authority speech is a perfect comedic gear-shift. It's lowbrow but structurally sound — the buildup of pomposity is punctured by the most undignified discovery possible. The word 'Doodie' itself is funnier than 'poop' by several degrees of juvenile charm.

jokes.text: Pool evacuation and candy bar confusion — the Baby Ruth visual gag
jokes.setup: Everyone panics over what appears to be feces floating in the pool after 'Doodie!' is shouted
jokes.punchline: It's revealed (or strongly implied by 'It's no big deal!') that the floating object is a candy bar (Baby Ruth), not actual excrement — classic Caddyshack bit inferred from context and dialogue
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most iconic gags. The misdirection is expertly sustained — the audience and characters both believe it's feces, the mass pool evacuation plays out in full comedic panic, and then the reveal deflates the horror into absurdity. The structure (setup panic → sustained commitment → deflating reveal) is textbook misdirection. Scores high on originality because few films have committed this hard to a poop/candy-bar fake-out at this scale.

jokes.text: I tried calling, but they don't have a listing for Mr. Wonderful. What spelling did you use?
jokes.setup: Lacey apologizes for showing up unannounced and explains she tried to call first
jokes.punchline: Ty asks 'What spelling did you use?' — accepting the absurd premise that 'Mr. Wonderful' might actually be his listed name and treating directory assistance as the obstacle
jokes.explanation: This is Chevy Chase at his most precisely calibrated. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a perfect deadpan non-sequitur, it reveals Ty's total unself-conscious ego, and the follow-up question ('What spelling?') commits fully to the absurdist logic rather than winking at the audience. Highly quotable, perfectly economical, and could only come from Ty's particular flavor of serene narcissism.

jokes.text: Would you like a drink? Tuna Colada, perhaps? / Who's your decorator? Benihana?
jokes.setup: Ty is showing Lacey around his eccentric home filled with aquatic/Vietnamese memorabilia
jokes.punchline: He offers a 'Tuna Colada' as a cocktail option, then Lacey clocks the décor and asks if Benihana (a Japanese restaurant chain) was the decorator — a deadpan dig at his chaotic aesthetic
jokes.explanation: Two quick jokes bundled together. 'Tuna Colada' is a pleasingly weird Ty-ism that fits his oceanic/absurdist personality. 'Benihana' is a sharp, economical insult from Lacey — specific enough to be funny, broad enough to land immediately. Neither is exceptional alone but they play well as a volley.

jokes.text: No, I brought most of that stuff back from Vietnam. / You were in the war? / Uh... no... Homo.
jokes.setup: Lacey asks if the decor came from Vietnam, assuming Ty served in the war
jokes.punchline: Ty corrects her: not Vietnam (the country/war), but 'Homo' — delivered with complete casualness as if the distinction is obvious, implying a restaurant or neighborhood called Homo
jokes.explanation: Classic Ty Webb non-answer. The deliberate pause before 'Homo' and the total nonchalance sell it as a Chevy Chase improv gem. The joke depends entirely on Ty's delivery — the character's breezy obliviousness makes a potentially edgy word read as pure absurdism rather than an insult.

jokes.text: Pretty pathetic, Ty. / Pathetic? Maybe for you, Lacey. For me, there's a subtle perfection in everything I do.
jokes.setup: Lacey finds uncashed checks for $70,000 and legal summonses scattered around Ty's chaotic home
jokes.punchline: Ty rejects the label 'pathetic' and replaces it with 'subtle perfection' — a magnificent self-delusion delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'subtle perfection in everything I do' is peak Ty Webb — it's his entire philosophy compressed into one line. The character integration score is high because this joke is utterly impossible without Ty's specific brand of Zen narcissism. It's also quotable as a standalone affirmation ironically.

jokes.text: My uncle says you've got a screw loose. / Your uncle molests collies.
jokes.setup: Lacey passes along her uncle's unflattering opinion of Ty
jokes.punchline: Ty volleys back with a specific, vivid counter-insult about the uncle and collies — delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'collies' (not just 'dogs') is what makes this land — it's so particular that it feels like actual intel rather than a generic insult. Ty's refusal to engage with the criticism and instead immediately going nuclear on the accuser is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: And you're rather... attractive for a... beautiful girl with a great body.
jokes.setup: Ty appears to be starting a backhanded compliment ('attractive for a...')
jokes.punchline: The expected insult pivot never comes — he completes the sentence with straight compliments, making the hesitations and pauses the joke rather than a twist
jokes.explanation: Smart structural reversal — the comedy comes from subverting the backhanded-compliment genre expectation. The audience braces for the insult and instead gets a sincere compliment delivered so awkwardly it still reads as strange. Very Ty: unable to deliver a normal sentence even when trying to flatter.

jokes.text: Ty sings an improvised 'love song' to Lacey including 'I was born to lick your face' and 'you were born to rub me first'
jokes.setup: Lacey asks Ty to sing her a love song
jokes.punchline: Ty delivers an increasingly bizarre improvised serenade with animal-ish, nonsensical romantic imagery
jokes.explanation: Chevy Chase improv energy — charming and weird but slightly unfocused. 'I was born to lick your face' is the highlight line; the rest is shaggy. Works because it's fully committed and in character, but the joke diffuses rather than builds to a clear punchline.

jokes.text: You know what this is called in the East? It's the big rub. / You're very... small-breasted. / No, I was kidding.
jokes.setup: Ty is giving Lacey a massage on the patio and narrating it with absurd Eastern-philosophy framing
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the massage narration, he observes 'You're very... small-breasted' — then immediately backtracks with 'No, I was kidding,' which makes it worse
jokes.explanation: The backtrack ('No, I was kidding') is the real punchline — an instant self-cancel that only deepens the awkwardness. Classic cringe structure: say the uncomfortable thing, then make it worse by trying to unsay it. Ty's total unawareness of social norms makes it character-consistent rather than gratuitously rude.

jokes.text: I'll work my way down. This is the Isle of Wight. Careful. I'm going to move right down the Ticonic Parkway... ...over to your clavula.
jokes.setup: Ty is narrating a massage using an increasingly absurd geography/anatomy hybrid tour-guide voice
jokes.punchline: 'Clavula' — a made-up anatomical term delivered with the same confidence as the real ones
jokes.explanation: The geography-as-body-tour bit is a sustained absurdist riff that gains momentum through accumulation. 'Clavula' as a fake word delivered with authority is the peak of the bit — it's the moment the audience realizes Ty has fully abandoned reality and is just making things up with total confidence.

jokes.text: It's like reaching under the rug, isn't it? / You're crazy! / That's what they said about Son of Sam.
jokes.setup: Ty says something inappropriate during the massage; Lacey calls him crazy
jokes.punchline: Ty responds 'That's what they said about Son of Sam' — equating himself with a serial killer as a casual deflection
jokes.explanation: Wildly dark reference deployed with casual breeziness — the gap between the gravity of Son of Sam and the trivial massage context is the entire joke. Ty's complete unflappability makes serial killer comparisons feel like compliments. Sharp economy, strong quotability.

jokes.text: I'm a very qualified acupuncturist. / Don't even think about it! / The slightest prick and you wouldn't even know...
jokes.setup: Ty claims to be a 'qualified acupuncturist' and starts talking about needles
jokes.punchline: 'The slightest prick and you wouldn't even know' — intentional double entendre delivered innocently
jokes.explanation: A functional double entendre that's fairly telegraphed. The setup ('acupuncture... prick') isn't surprising but Ty's breezy obliviousness to the double meaning gives it some character grounding. Mid-tier — gets a chuckle but not a big laugh.

jokes.text: You feel looser? / I feel like a 100 dollars.
jokes.setup: After the chaotic massage/acupuncture session, Ty asks if she feels better
jokes.punchline: She says 'I feel like a 100 dollars' — a deliberate downgrade of 'a million dollars,' implying the massage was underwhelming
jokes.explanation: The deflation of 'a million dollars' to 'a hundred dollars' is a neat, economical joke. Specific enough to be more interesting than 'I feel terrible.' The understated delivery implied makes it land as dry wit from Lacey.

jokes.text: Will you forget the massage and just kiss me, you fool.
jokes.setup: After all of Ty's absurd massage/acupuncture shenanigans, Lacey has had enough of his diversions
jokes.punchline: She cuts through all the nonsense with a bluntly direct command, calling him 'you fool' — the most grounded and exasperated line in a surreal scene
jokes.explanation: Works as a comedic exhale after the sustained absurdity of the massage scene. 'You fool' is the right word — affectionate but exasperated, cutting through Ty's performance with a straight line that gets a laugh through contrast.

jokes.text: Hey, what kind of shit is this? / It's the best, man. I got it from a Negro.
jokes.setup: Caddies are smoking marijuana and one questions the quality
jokes.punchline: The endorsement 'I got it from a Negro' is offered as the definitive quality proof — a period-specific, bluntly casual racial shorthand that's played for the character's oblivious naivety
jokes.explanation: The joke is meant to characterize the speaker as naively racist rather than to endorse the sentiment — it's played as oblivious cluelessness. By 1980 standards this reads as satirical character work; by contemporary standards it lands uneasily. The craft is functional but the humor relies partly on shock rather than wit, hence a below-average earned_vs_cheap score.

jokes.text: He looks like Dick Cavett.
jokes.setup: Caddies are high and looking at someone (presumably a stoned, blank-faced companion)
jokes.punchline: The only observation one stoned caddy can muster is that he resembles the mild-mannered talk show host Dick Cavett — the most specific and least flattering comparison imaginable
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Dick Cavett' out of all possible celebrities is what makes this work — it's so oddly precise that it feels like genuine stoned-brain logic. A single non-sequitur line perfectly capturing the high, meandering caddy vibe.

jokes.text: Ahoy, polloi. What did you just come from, a Scotch ad?
jokes.setup: Al Czervik arrives at the dock where Judge Smails and company are dressed in preppy nautical attire for the boat christening
jokes.punchline: He greets them as 'polloi' (riffing on 'hoi polloi') and immediately insults their coordinated WASP outfits as looking like a Scotch whiskey advertisement
jokes.explanation: 'Ahoy, polloi' is a perfect double-layered joke: a nautical greeting + a class-based inversion of 'hoi polloi,' suggesting Smails and crew are the common rabble despite their pretensions. 'Scotch ad' is the ideal visual insult for WASPy nautical fashion. This is Rodney Dangerfield operating at his sharpest — class warfare compressed into a greeting.

jokes.text: My, what a nice looking young man! You're from Bushwood, aren't you? / He's not a member, Grandma. He's a caddy!
jokes.setup: Smails's grandmother compliments Danny Noonan, assuming he's a club member
jokes.punchline: Smails corrects her with barely concealed horror — 'He's a caddy!' — revealing how catastrophic the social confusion is in his world
jokes.explanation: Classic class-comedy beat. The grandmother's oblivious friendliness versus Smails's class-anxious horror makes the joke. Works through character contrast — her warmth exposes his snobbery.

jokes.text: Well, you two look like a couple of boogies. Why don't you just scamper along now?
jokes.setup: Smails wants Al Czervik and Danny to leave the dock area
jokes.punchline: He calls them 'boogies' and tells them to 'scamper' — using condescending language that reveals his pomposity while undercutting his own authority by sounding ridiculous
jokes.explanation: Smails insulting people while thinking he's dignified is consistent character comedy. 'Scamper' is an odd, funny word choice that makes him sound more absurd than authoritative.

jokes.text: I'm going to law school, too. / Really? Are you going to Harvard? / No. St. Copius of, uh, Northern... / Where?
jokes.setup: Danny tries to establish credentials by mentioning he's going to law school
jokes.punchline: He can't even remember the name of his school ('St. Copius of, uh, Northern...'), deflating his own social-climbing attempt completely
jokes.explanation: The trailing-off mid-name is a perfect character detail — Danny is so out of his depth that he can't even commit to his own comeback. The simple 'Where?' follow-up is a killing blow delivered with minimal effort.

jokes.text: Hey, Cary Grant. You want to get high? / Wait a minute. I've only got a little. / Then split. Okay?
jokes.setup: Al Czervik is approached by a stoned caddy who offers to share his weed
jokes.punchline: Al accepts enthusiastically, the caddy reveals he 'only has a little,' and Al immediately says 'Then split. Okay?' — cutting off the interaction the moment it stops being useful
jokes.explanation: Al's instant dismissal — zero social grace, pure transactional logic — is a great character beat. 'Cary Grant' as a nickname for the stoned kid is an inspired throwaway. The speed of the rejection is what sells it; Dangerfield doesn't waste a beat.

jokes.text: Guess I'm a little overdressed, huh? / Depends on what's underneath.
jokes.setup: Lacey arrives at the dock and self-consciously notes she might be overdressed for the occasion
jokes.punchline: Al volleys back with 'Depends on what's underneath' — a double entendre that's both a compliment and an innuendo
jokes.explanation: Functional Dangerfield innuendo — fast, economical, gets the job done. The double meaning is fairly predictable but delivered with enough snap to land. Mid-tier joke from a character capable of better.

jokes.text: Judge Smails recites a poem: 'It's easy to grin when your ship comes in... but the man worthwhile is the man who can smile when his shorts are too tight in the seat!'
jokes.setup: Smails announces he has a poem for the boat christening, the crowd expects a dignified verse
jokes.punchline: The poem ends with 'when his shorts are too tight in the seat' — a grotesquely undignified punchline delivered by the most pompous man at the club with total self-seriousness
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best jokes. The structure is classically perfect: a pompous man reciting a poem at a formal occasion, the verse sounds like it's building to something wise and inspirational, then 'when his shorts are too tight in the seat' arrives with full comic force. The deflation from faux-wisdom to groin discomfort is immaculate, and Smails delivers it without a trace of irony — he genuinely believes this is profound. High marks across the board: original in its specificity, perfectly structured, completely character-dependent, and deeply quotable. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in its escalation-deflation structure.

jokes.text: This is your fate line. Looks like you're going to make a lot of money when you're older. Oh, yeah? When? How? Could be in the market... or on a game show.
jokes.setup: Ty is reading Lacey's palm, delivering mystical pronouncements about her fate
jokes.punchline: 'Could be in the market... or on a game show' — the mystic vision collapses into banal, completely unimpressive possibilities, with 'game show' being the deflating final option
jokes.explanation: The 'or on a game show' landing is the essence of Ty Webb — he starts with gravitas and slides effortlessly into something completely unworthy of gravitas. The casualness of the pivot is the joke. Well-constructed deflation.

jokes.text: And this is your saliva line. / What does it tell? / How hot I can get you.
jokes.setup: Ty continues the fake palm reading, tracing another line and labeling it
jokes.punchline: 'Saliva line' is not a real palm-reading term; its 'meaning' is a blatant come-on rather than any mystical insight
jokes.explanation: Very economical Chevy Chase move — inventing 'saliva line' as a fake palm term is creative, and the payoff ('how hot I can get you') is direct and confident. The invented pseudo-scientific term is funnier than any real one would be.

jokes.text: My dinghy is bigger than your whole boat!
jokes.setup: Al has taken over the yacht and is now taunting from the water
jokes.punchline: 'My dinghy is bigger than your whole boat' — a size boast that works as both literal boat comparison and barely-concealed anatomical bragging
jokes.explanation: Economical Dangerfield line that works on two levels. The literal reading (his actual tender boat is larger than the yacht) is itself absurd; the innuendo layer is a bonus. Very quotable, delivered with Dangerfield's typical machine-gun confidence.

jokes.text: I almost got head from Amelia Earhart!
jokes.setup: Al is driving the yacht recklessly and nearly collides with something or someone
jokes.punchline: He celebrates a near-miss by claiming he 'almost got head from Amelia Earhart' — the most unexpected celebrity reference possible, involving a long-dead aviation pioneer
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best Dangerfield lines. The specificity of Amelia Earhart (not a generic old woman — a specific historical figure known for disappearing) creates the joke's texture. The collision between crude language ('got head') and a dignified historical figure is jarring and funny. It's also absurdist: how is Amelia Earhart at this lake? The line doesn't explain itself and doesn't need to. Comparable in economy and surprise to the 8.0 anchor example.

jokes.text: What is this? Hell's Angels?
jokes.setup: Al's chaotic boat arrival has caused mayhem at the docks.
jokes.punchline: Judge Smails's horrified comparison of a boat crash to a biker gang rumble — the pompous panic at disrupted propriety.
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction line — the disproportionate comparison is consistent with Smails's melodramatic snobbery. Not particularly clever but serves the scene rhythm.

jokes.text: Back! / Which way is backwards?
jokes.setup: Chaos on the water; someone is trying to direct the boat away from danger
jokes.punchline: Al, having commandeered a boat he can't operate, earnestly asks 'Which way is backwards?' — revealing total incompetence with no shame
jokes.explanation: Al's total confidence in seizing control combined with his total inability to actually operate the boat is consistent and funny. 'Which way is backwards?' lands because it's such a basic question from someone who just took command so aggressively.

jokes.text: Hey, you scratched my anchor!
jokes.setup: Al has just caused a boating collision/disaster while driving recklessly
jokes.punchline: In the aftermath of the crash he caused, Al complains that his anchor got scratched — total inversion of responsibility, playing the victim of his own destruction
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Dangerfield. The setup is the entire boating disaster, and the punchline is Al's complete moral inversion — he caused the damage but complains about his own scratch as if he's the wronged party. Character integration is high because this exact move (causing chaos, then immediately acting aggrieved) is Al Czervik's comedic DNA.

jokes.text: I just want you to know that because of this... you don't have to stop seeing other people.
jokes.setup: Post-intimacy moment between Ty and Lacey; the conventional line would be romantic reassurance or commitment
jokes.punchline: Ty offers the reverse of the expected — not 'you're mine now' but 'this doesn't mean anything, please keep seeing other people' — delivered with his characteristic Zen detachment
jokes.explanation: One of the best Ty Webb lines in the film. The post-coital moment is perfectly subverted — instead of possessiveness or romance, Ty offers detached permission for continued promiscuity, framed as a considerate gesture. It's funny, character-perfect, and captures his entire philosophy (non-attachment, lack of ego investment) in one line. Highly quotable as a standalone.

jokes.text: Are we still having tea? / Will you come and loofah my stretch marks?
jokes.setup: Judge Smails is soaking wet and furious after the boating disaster Al caused
jokes.punchline: His wife's first concern is tea, and her second request is for him to loofah her stretch marks — both wildly incongruous with the chaos, delivered with complete oblivious domesticity
jokes.explanation: 'Loofah my stretch marks' is a great specific detail — the mundane grotesquerie of it cuts perfectly against the pompous boat-christening disaster. The incongruity of domestic banality following a minor catastrophe is well-executed.

jokes.text: Carl Spackler's lawn-mowing fantasy: 'What an incredible Cinderella story! This unknown comes out of nowhere...' narrated over his own solo golf swing in an empty field
jokes.setup: Carl is mowing the lawn alone
jokes.punchline: He provides his own ecstatic golf-broadcast commentary while playing an imaginary Masters tournament in his head, treating his mundane groundskeeping as an epic sporting moment
jokes.explanation: One of the most beloved moments in the film and in Bill Murray's career. The extended monologue — Carl narrating his own fantasy Masters victory while mowing grass — is a masterpiece of character comedy. It works on every level: it's completely in character (Carl's grandiose delusions about his golf skills and place in the world), it escalates beautifully ('former greenskeeper now about to become the Masters champion'), and 'It's in the hole!' has become a cultural touchstone. The structure — building through stadium noise and crowd reactions to a climactic putt — is tightly constructed despite being delivered as an improvised ramble. This is what 8.5+ looks like.

jokes.text: It's in the hole!
jokes.setup: Carl has narrated an entire imaginary golf tournament to himself while mowing; the fantasy climaxes with a final putt
jokes.punchline: 'It's in the hole!' — the triumphant peak of his self-broadcast, delivered with ecstatic release
jokes.explanation: Four words that became one of the most quoted lines in sports/comedy film history. Scored separately from the full monologue because it functions as the culminating punchline — the payoff to the extended escalation. 'It's in the hole!' has an economy score of 10 because it cannot be shorter and delivers maximum impact. It earns its cultural status: the contrast between the grandeur of Carl's fantasy and the reality of a groundskeeper mowing grass is never funnier than at this peak moment.

jokes.text: I was hoping to squeeze in nine holes before this rain starts. / Certainly, Your Eminency. Take my bag, huh?
jokes.setup: A Bishop of the Church arrives to play golf, wanting to get in a round before a storm
jokes.punchline: He immediately hands his clubs to Danny with the casual authority of someone who treats everyone as his servant — 'Your Eminency' said with reverence, followed instantly by being used as a caddy
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the Bishop subplot. The comedy is in the character type — a man of God whose primary passion is golf, and who imperiously drafts a stranger as his caddy mid-conversation. Functional but mostly setup work for bigger payoffs to come.

jokes.text: Nice shot, Bishop. You must have made a deal with the devil!
jokes.setup: The Bishop hits an amazing golf shot despite deteriorating storm conditions
jokes.punchline: Danny jokes that the Bishop made a deal with the devil — a funny theological inversion: the man of God succeeding suspiciously well
jokes.explanation: A solid ironic joke — telling a Bishop he's in league with the devil is a good inversion. The setup (miraculous shot in impossible conditions) earns it. Not extraordinary but clean.

jokes.text: So what do you think? / I'd keep playing. I don't think the heavy stuff is going to come down for quite a while. / The good Lord would never disrupt the best game of my life.
jokes.setup: A severe storm is visibly developing; Danny asks the Bishop whether they should stop
jokes.punchline: The Bishop reasons that God wouldn't interrupt his best golf game — a stunning display of divine self-importance from a religious figure
jokes.explanation: The Bishop's theology is entirely self-serving: God won't disrupt his golf game because God wouldn't dare. This is excellent character comedy — the man of God whose faith is entirely devoted to the proposition that the Almighty is personally invested in his golf score. Sets up the inevitable lightning payoff perfectly. High character integration because this exact brand of pious self-importance is the Bishop's defining trait.

jokes.text: ...the good Lord would never disrupt the... ...best game of my life.
jokes.setup: Thunder and lightning are building; Danny urges the Bishop to come in from the storm.
jokes.punchline: The Bishop asserts that God would never ruin his round of golf — the theological hubris of claiming divine intervention on behalf of one's personal athletic achievement.
jokes.explanation: The setup of the Bishop's hubris is elegant — he's not a bad man, just completely lost in golf obsession. The irony that God is about to strike him with lightning immediately after he claims divine protection is a classic comic structure. The pause before 'best game of my life' is perfectly placed.

jokes.text: I'm infallible, young fellow!
jokes.setup: Danny expresses doubt about playing in the worsening storm
jokes.punchline: The Bishop declares himself 'infallible' — a papal claim that belongs to the Pope, not a Bishop, making him both theologically wrong and comically arrogant
jokes.explanation: A brilliant little theological joke hiding inside a character bit. 'Infallible' is specifically a papal doctrine — a Bishop claiming infallibility is not only arrogant but doctrinally incorrect, which layers the comedy for anyone who catches it. Even without the theological knowledge, the sheer pomposity of claiming infallibility mid-golf-game is funny. This is the kind of joke that rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Ratfarts!
jokes.setup: The Bishop, who has been invoking the Lord's protection and declaring his infallibility, hits a bad shot (or is hit by lightning)
jokes.punchline: His eruption: 'Ratfarts!' — the most undignified expletive possible from a man of the cloth
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the entire Bishop sequence. Everything built to this: his pious certainty that God backed his golf game, his claim of infallibility, Danny's doubts — all of it collapses into 'Ratfarts!' The word itself is inspired: it's not a real swear word (so it's simultaneously mild and absurd), but coming from a Bishop it's as scandalous as any profanity. The economy score is 10 because one word destroys an entire pretentious edifice. This rivals 'It's in the hole!' for the reel's most iconic single-word punchline.

jokes.text: Late for what? / For not being pregnant!
jokes.setup: Maggie says she's 'late'; Danny asks what she's late for, expecting a mundane answer
jokes.punchline: 'For not being pregnant' — the revelation that 'late' means her period, delivered as a correction of his naivety
jokes.explanation: Structurally very clean — the setup exploits the dual meaning of 'late' perfectly, letting the audience and Danny both process the innocent reading before the punchline lands. 'For not being pregnant' is a funny formulation: technically 'late for not being pregnant' doesn't quite make logical sense, which makes it funnier and more panicked-sounding. High economy, great structure.

jokes.text: We'll just get married. / Oh, God! That's all I need!
jokes.setup: Danny tries to be noble and suggests they get married to handle the pregnancy
jokes.punchline: Maggie's instant, horrified rejection: 'Oh, God! That's all I need!' — treating marriage to Danny as a catastrophe worse than the pregnancy itself
jokes.explanation: The reversal of expected roles — the man proposing nobly, the woman rejecting with horror — is well-executed. 'That's all I need!' suggests being pregnant is manageable but being married to Danny would be the real disaster, which is both funny and a sharp character indictment.

jokes.text: It might not be yours. Okay?
jokes.setup: Danny keeps insisting on marrying Maggie; she needs to shut down his persistence
jokes.punchline: She reveals the baby might not be his — not as a dramatic confession but as a casual conversational card played to end the argument
jokes.explanation: The 'Okay?' at the end makes this — it's so casual, so matter-of-fact, as if revealing possible paternity ambiguity is just a conversational speed bump. The tone is the joke: a potentially devastating revelation deployed as an annoyance-deflector.

jokes.text: I know you're just making this up about the other guys so I won't have to feel guilty. / I'm not making it up! / All right. Well, I'm still willing to marry you!
jokes.setup: Maggie confesses the baby may not be Danny's; Danny refuses to believe it
jokes.punchline: Danny magnanimously offers to marry her anyway despite the revelation — his self-delusion ('you're just saying that') followed by his oblivious nobility is a double comic beat
jokes.explanation: Danny's insistence that Maggie is lying to protect his feelings — when she's telling the truth — is good character comedy. His follow-up 'Well, I'm still willing to marry you!' after learning it might not be his child at all is a great escalation of his misguided nobility.

jokes.text: Well, thanks for nothing!
jokes.setup: Danny has just heroically offered to marry Maggie despite everything — clearly proud of himself
jokes.punchline: Maggie's flat, withering 'Well, thanks for nothing!' — his gallantry lands as an insult
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the scene. Danny's sincere offer of marriage is so inadequate — so presumptuous and self-congratulatory — that Maggie's flat dismissal is exactly right. 'Thanks for nothing' captures the whole dynamic: she doesn't want his help, his offer insulted her independence, and she won't even give him credit for trying. Economy score is high — four words close an entire scene.

jokes.text: My niece is the kind of girl that has a certain... zest for living.
jokes.setup: Judge Smails is meeting privately with Danny about the incident with his niece (Lacey)
jokes.punchline: 'Zest for living' as a euphemism for promiscuity — Smails's pompous verbal dancing around Lacey's sexual behavior
jokes.explanation: The euphemism works perfectly for Smails — a man who cannot say anything plainly if there's a pompous circumlocution available. 'Zest for living' is the ideal cover phrase: it's aspirational, positive, and completely avoids the actual subject.

jokes.text: I've sentenced boys younger than you to the gas chamber. I didn't want to do it. I felt I owed it to them.
jokes.setup: Judge Smails is lecturing Danny about goodness vs. badness, presenting himself as a moral authority
jokes.punchline: 'I felt I owed it to them' — an absurd framing of sentencing young men to death as a service he performed for their benefit
jokes.explanation: One of the darkest and best jokes in the film. The structure is perfect: Smails presents himself as a reluctant but conscientious executioner, the slight hesitation ('I didn't want to do it'), then the kicker — 'I felt I owed it to them' — which inverts the horror into an act of generosity. The self-serving logic is monstrous and hilarious. Ted Knight delivers this with absolute sincerity, which makes it land even harder. Comparable in darkness and craft to the best anchors — the character integration is 9.0 because only Smails could frame capital punishment as a favor.

jokes.text: Why, just ask my grandson, Spaulding. He and I are regular pals. Are you my pal? Mister Scholarship Winner?
jokes.setup: Smails is trying to sell Danny on his warmth and approachability, citing his relationship with his grandson as evidence
jokes.punchline: He turns to Danny with 'Are you my pal?' — an infantilizing question delivered to an adult young man, with the patronizing kicker 'Mister Scholarship Winner' that underscores how completely Smails holds the power here
jokes.explanation: The cringe here is real — Smails forcing Danny to perform friendship ('Are you my pal?') while holding the scholarship over him. 'Mister Scholarship Winner' drips with condescension. Ted Knight's particular brand of insidious pomposity makes this land as deeply uncomfortable comedy.

jokes.text: How about a Fresca?
jokes.setup: Smails has just conducted an intimidating private meeting — gas chambers, moral lectures, 'are you my pal?' — and now needs to close the encounter
jokes.punchline: He offers Danny a Fresca — the most anticlimactic possible hospitality gesture after an intense power-play meeting
jokes.explanation: One of the great comic non-sequiturs in the film. 'Fresca' — a mid-tier grapefruit soda — is the precise right choice here: not water (too humble), not Scotch (too friendly), but Fresca, which is both specific and oddly deflating. The transition from gas chamber threats to 'How about a Fresca?' is a tonal whiplash that generates a huge laugh. Economy is 10: three words close the entire intimidation scene with a puncturing comedy beat. Ted Knight's earnest delivery makes it land perfectly.

jokes.text: You never ask a navy man if he'll have another drink... because it's nobody's goddamn business how many drinks he's had already, right? / Wrong! You're drinking too much, Your Excellency.
jokes.setup: The Bishop is offered another drink and launches into a 'navy man' code about never being questioned on drinking
jokes.punchline: His monologue is immediately flatly contradicted by whoever's with him — 'Wrong! You're drinking too much, Your Excellency' — deflating the naval philosophy instantly
jokes.explanation: The Bishop's self-justifying philosophy about navy drinking culture is itself funny, then the flat 'Wrong!' is the punchline. The pattern (man explains his elaborate excuse for behavior → immediate dismissal) works cleanly.

jokes.text: Excellency... fiddlesticks! My name is Fred and I'm just a man, same as you are. / You're not a man. You're a Bishop, for God's sake! / There is no God!
jokes.setup: The drunk Bishop is insisting on being treated as an ordinary person named Fred
jokes.punchline: When corrected that he is in fact a Bishop, he responds 'There is no God!' — a cascade of escalating theological abandonment
jokes.explanation: The escalation is perfect: Bishop insists he's just 'Fred' → told he's a Bishop → 'There is no God!' The drunk Bishop's theological collapse happens in three rapid steps, each more extreme than the last. The final leap to atheism as a response to being reminded of his own ecclesiastical rank is both absurd and logically coherent in a drunken way. This is excellent escalation comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, Webb, I didn't see your name on the sign-in sheet for the Club tournament. I thought you'd be the man to beat this year. Guess you'll just have to keep beating yourself.
jokes.setup: Smails sidles up to Ty Webb to deliver a pointed observation about him not entering the club tournament
jokes.punchline: 'Guess you'll just have to keep beating yourself' — ostensibly about golf practice, with an unmistakable masturbation implication that Smails delivers seemingly without awareness
jokes.explanation: The joke works perfectly because it's ambiguous whether Smails intends the double meaning. If he's oblivious, it's a classic case of a pompous man accidentally insulting himself with a crude innuendo while trying to be cutting. If he intends it, it's out of character. The former reading is funnier and more consistent. 'Beating yourself' as a double entendre delivered in Smails's pompous register is a great collision of register and content.

jokes.text: You have worn out your welcome, sir! / Is that so? Who made you Pope of this dump?
jokes.setup: Smails formally declares Al has worn out his welcome at the club
jokes.punchline: Al deflects with 'Who made you Pope of this dump?' — a great counter-insult that (a) undercuts Smails's authority, (b) calls the club a dump, and (c) bonus: 'Pope' echoes the Bishop subplot running in this reel
jokes.explanation: One of Dangerfield's best lines in the film. The word 'Pope' is exactly right — it's the most grandiose possible authority figure, making Smails seem ridiculous for lording over a golf club. Calling Bushwood a 'dump' in the same breath is a double insult in one economical question. Character integration is high because this exact move — immediately flipping from accused to accuser — is classic Czervik.

jokes.text: Are you kidding? You think I'd join this crummy snobatorium? Why, this whole place sucks! The only reason I'm here is maybe I'll buy it!
jokes.setup: Smails threatens Al will never be a member at Bushwood
jokes.punchline: Al escalates past the insult to announce he doesn't want to join — he's going to BUY the whole place, delivering his ultimate trump card
jokes.explanation: 'Snobatorium' is a perfect invented word — it compounds 'snob' and 'sanatorium,' implying Bushwood is both a place for snobs and an institution for the mentally disturbed. The escalation from 'I wouldn't join' to 'I might BUY it' is perfect Czervik: he doesn't just win arguments, he makes the entire premise of the argument irrelevant. This is a key character-defining moment for Al.

jokes.text: He tried to choke me! / And he called me a baboon. Thinks I'm his wife.
jokes.setup: An altercation has broken out; both men are filing complaints simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Al's complaint — 'He called me a baboon. Thinks I'm his wife' — is the funnier filing: the baboon insult is bad enough, but Al's addition 'Thinks I'm his wife' implies Smails calls his wife a baboon, which is an insult absorbed without being directly spoken
jokes.explanation: The 'Thinks I'm his wife' kicker is clever — it implies a whole backstory (Smails calls Mrs. Smails a baboon) without stating it, and it casts Mrs. Smails as an accidental victim of the insult. Great economy in the construction.

jokes.text: He tried to choke me! You saw it. / And he called me a baboon. Thinks I'm his wife.
jokes.setup: Judge Smails is reporting to onlookers what Al did to him.
jokes.punchline: 'Thinks I'm his wife' — the addendum that Al called him a baboon AND believes him to be his wife escalates the insult to absurdist heights.
jokes.explanation: 'Thinks I'm his wife' is the unexpected escalation — the baboon comparison is a standard insult, but the spousal confusion is an absurdist detail that makes it funnier and weirder. Good economy on the follow-up line.

jokes.text: You can call the chief of police! I built his condo!
jokes.setup: Someone threatens to call the police on Al
jokes.punchline: Al is unbothered: he built the police chief's condo — implying he owns the chief's loyalty through real estate
jokes.explanation: Al's power is built on real estate connections — this line perfectly encapsulates his world: he doesn't respect institutional authority because he's bought it. 'I built his condo' as an instant police-threat deflection is perfectly economical and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Are you flipping out? / No. I'm happy! I'm not pregnant!
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Maggie is 'flipping out' — implying she's upset or behaving erratically
jokes.punchline: She clarifies she's happy because she's NOT pregnant, recontextualizing her emotional state as relief at a near-miss disaster
jokes.explanation: Sharp misdirection — the audience expects emotional distress, gets relief at a potentially life-altering near-miss. The pregnancy callback pays off a subplot thread efficiently. Not exceptional but solid structural work.

jokes.text: No, I've been a creep lately and I just can't help it. / You're not a creep. / Yes, I am. / No, you're not. / All right, maybe you are a little bit.
jokes.setup: Maggie reassures Danny he's not a creep in a classic 'you're not bad' back-and-forth
jokes.punchline: After the obligatory denial, Maggie breaks the pattern and concedes: 'All right, maybe you are a little bit.'
jokes.explanation: Classic beat subversion — the reassurance ritual runs its expected course and then collapses hilariously when Maggie drops the act. Economy and timing are the craft here. Not original but well-executed.

jokes.text: I demand satisfaction! / Oh, you want satisfaction. / I'll tell you what's real satisfying. Cash! / I'll shoot you 18 holes for 10,000 bucks.
jokes.setup: Judge Smails issues a pompous formal challenge: 'I demand satisfaction!' — evoking dueling language and wounded aristocratic pride
jokes.punchline: Czervik immediately deflates the grandeur: 'I'll tell you what's real satisfying. Cash!' — turning a matter of honor into crass commerce
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures the central class-war comedy engine of the film. Smails's pomposity is punctured instantly by Czervik's nouveau-riche vulgarity. The character integration is excellent — only Czervik could respond this way. Economy is tight and the pivot from dueling honor to dollars is a great comic deflation.

jokes.text: Why, I could beat you with one arm.
jokes.setup: Smails is being challenged to a golf match by the man he despises
jokes.punchline: His boast that he could beat Czervik with one arm — delivered with absolute imperious conviction — is funny because it's so inflated and will soon be tested
jokes.explanation: Modest gag but gains value as foreshadowing — his arm DOES get broken later, making this a subtle callback setup. Character-specific bluster. Not especially original but functions in the narrative.

jokes.text: How about teams for $20,000? You can have Dr. Frankenputz.
jokes.setup: Czervik is proposing a team match and needs to assign partners
jokes.punchline: 'Dr. Frankenputz' — a portmanteau nickname for the pompous club doctor, blending Frankenstein with 'putz' (Yiddish for idiot/fool) and 'putts'
jokes.explanation: Triple-layered wordplay in two syllables: Frankenstein (the monster), putz (Yiddish insult perfectly in Czervik's Jewish-outsider voice), and putts (golf). Exceptional economy — it insults both the character and his golf game simultaneously. Highly quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: I beg your pardon! [reaction to being called Dr. Frankenputz]
jokes.setup: Czervik has just coined the nickname 'Dr. Frankenputz' for the stuffy club doctor
jokes.punchline: The doctor's flustered 'I beg your pardon!' — the classic British/aristocratic expression of outrage — is exactly the reaction that makes the insult land harder
jokes.explanation: The straight-man reaction that completes the Frankenputz joke. Functional but generic — the punchline belongs to Czervik. This is just the echo.

jokes.text: I don't play golf for money... against people.
jokes.setup: Everyone is pressuring Ty to join the money match; the natural completion is 'I don't play golf for money' (a principled refusal)
jokes.punchline: The addition of '...against people' implies he DOES play golf for money — just not against humans. It's a perfect Zen-eccentric non-sequitur that is entirely Ty Webb.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. Perfectly calibrated to Ty Webb's established character — the aloof, Zen-golfer whose relationship with reality is slightly off-kilter. The pause before 'against people' is structural genius: it allows the audience to think they know the end of the sentence and then subverts it completely. It raises more questions than it answers (who DOES he play for money against?) while being completely in character. High quotability, works on rewatch as you anticipate the pause. Comparable to the 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' anchor in its economy and unexpectedness.

jokes.text: Are you religious or something? / You might say that.
jokes.setup: Czervik tries to categorize Ty's refusal to play for money with the only framework he understands — religion
jokes.punchline: Ty's cryptic 'You might say that' — neither confirming nor denying, perfectly maintaining his inscrutable persona
jokes.explanation: A coda to the superior '...against people' joke. Ty's non-answer maintains his mystique. Czervik's attempt to pin down what can't be pinned down is good character comedy. Dependent on the previous joke's energy.

jokes.text: Your father and I prepped together...went to war together, played golf together. We built this club, he and I! Let's face it. Some people...simply do not belong.
jokes.setup: Smails pulls Ty aside for a private word, invoking his father's memory and their deep shared history to build gravitas
jokes.punchline: After all this solemn buildup, the destination is simply: 'Some people simply do not belong.' — naked class snobbery dressed in borrowed prestige
jokes.explanation: Classic Smails comedy — pompous buildup to naked classism. The whole speech is a vehicle to deliver a verdict he could have stated in two words. The gap between his self-importance and his pettiness is where the humor lives. Character-specific and thematically resonant.

jokes.text: Let's not... cave in too easy, huh?
jokes.setup: Smails has just made his pompous classist appeal; the expected response is agreement or refusal
jokes.punchline: Ty's breezy, mild counter — 'let's not cave in too easy' — treats the whole class-war drama as a minor negotiation, undermining Smails's gravity
jokes.explanation: Ty treating Smails's heartfelt appeal as barely worth engaging with is funny and character-consistent. The pause implied in '...cave in too easy' suggests he's considered it for about half a second before deciding against it.

jokes.text: My dad... never liked you.
jokes.setup: Smails has invoked Ty's late father as the cornerstone of his appeal — 'Your father and I prepped together, went to war together...'
jokes.punchline: After agreeing to raise the stakes to $40,000, Ty's parting shot: 'My dad... never liked you.' — demolishing everything Smails built in one beat
jokes.explanation: A devastating callback delivered with perfect Ty Webb nonchalance. Smails spends 45 seconds constructing a monument to their shared history and Ty demolishes it with five words and a pause. The ellipsis before 'never liked you' is crucial — it mimics Smails's own portentous style and then weaponizes it. This is excellent comedy writing: callback, character-specific voice, perfect economy, and a thematic gut-punch dressed as a casual aside. Earns its 8+ score.

jokes.text: I have to laugh...because I've often asked myself...My foe, my enemy, is an animal...and in order to conquer him...I have to think like an animal. And whenever possible...to look like one.
jokes.setup: Carl is apparently delivering a monologue to himself (or to animal props) about his gopher-hunting strategy
jokes.punchline: 'And whenever possible...to look like one.' — the logical progression from thinking like an animal to looking like one, delivered with complete Apocalypse Now-style solemnity
jokes.explanation: Bill Murray improvising a military-tactical monologue about fighting a gopher is exactly the character and exactly the film. The parody of Apocalypse Now / war-movie solemnity applied to lawn pest control is funny throughout, and 'to look like one' is a genuinely surprising logical extension. Carl is the most fully comedic character in the film and this is a showcase moment.

jokes.text: I've got to get inside...this dude's hole and crawl around for a few days.
jokes.setup: Carl continues his gopher-hunting war-room monologue
jokes.punchline: The completely unironic plan to crawl into the gopher's hole and live there for days — delivered with tactical confidence
jokes.explanation: The absurd logic escalates nicely — not just think like the enemy, but physically occupy his space. 'This dude's hole' is a funny clash of register (tactical military + casual stoner). Part of a sustained comic monologue rather than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Who is the gopher's ally? His friend? The harmless squirrel and the friendly rabbit. I'm going to use you guys to do my dirty work for me.
jokes.setup: Carl, fully in his tactical delusion, is addressing actual stuffed/toy animals (or live ones) as if conducting a war briefing
jokes.punchline: He recruits a squirrel and rabbit as covert operatives, addressing them directly with strategic intent
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Carl has enlisted woodland creatures as intelligence assets is a perfect absurdist escalation. The formal register — 'I'm going to use you guys to do my dirty work' — applied to a rabbit is classic Carl. Sets up the plastic explosives gag.

jokes.text: This is it! It's the Title! [Carl apparently finds the gopher hole and reacts as if achieving a great victory]
jokes.setup: Carl has been hunting the gopher obsessively; he finally locates what he believes is the gopher's main tunnel
jokes.punchline: He announces it like a championship moment — 'It's the Title!' — treating lawn pest control as the Super Bowl
jokes.explanation: Modest but character-consistent. The inflation of a gopher hunt to championship-level stakes is the central Carl joke, repeated here with diminishing returns from earlier moments but still functional.

jokes.text: All right, show yourself, you little varmint! If you've got the guts. Son of a bitch. Where did you go? Oh, hi, Carl.
jokes.setup: Carl is alone on the course raging at the gopher in the dark; the audience assumes he's alone in his delusion
jokes.punchline: The abrupt pivot to 'Oh, hi, Carl' reveals Ty Webb was there watching; it's Ty greeting himself (or Carl greeting Ty whose name happens to be... wait — Ty's surname isn't Carl). Actually this is Carl being greeted by Ty who calls him Carl. The joke is the instant deflation from full gopher-combat mode to casual social greeting.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. Carl is at maximum intensity — screaming curses at a gopher — and then snaps instantly into polite social mode. The juxtaposition of 'Son of a bitch' and 'Oh, hi, Carl' in consecutive beats is a great tonal whiplash. Character comedy working at a high level.

jokes.text: Mind if I play through? / Sure. Go right ahead.
jokes.setup: It's the middle of the night; Carl has been raging at a gopher hole in the dark
jokes.punchline: Ty asks to 'play through' as if this were a normal round of golf, and Carl obligingly agrees as if this were perfectly normal
jokes.explanation: Ty's completely casual request to play through in pitch dark, while Carl is waging psychological warfare on a rodent, is a perfect deadpan absurdity. Both men treat this as normal golf etiquette, which makes it funnier. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Carl's shack interior — Ty's reaction: 'It's really awful.'
jokes.setup: Carl has seemingly invited Ty into his home/shack, possibly proud of it; Ty looks around
jokes.punchline: Ty's flat, sincere 'It's really awful.' — no diplomacy, no cushioning
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ty Webb line — absolute honesty without cruelty. The economy is stellar ('It's really awful' vs. any longer version). Works because Ty is too Zen to bother with social niceties.

jokes.text: It's really awful. / Well, I have a lot of things on order. You know, credit trouble. I'm an assistant greenskeeper.
jokes.setup: Ty has been invited into Carl's shack/home and observes the squalor
jokes.punchline: Carl's explanation for the awful conditions is 'credit trouble' and the status update that he is merely an 'assistant' greenskeeper — a job that pays almost nothing — delivered as if these are minor logistical hiccups
jokes.explanation: Carl's cheerful poverty and his explanation of his career trajectory are funny in context. 'Credit trouble' as the reason your home is 'really awful' is a great understatement. The visual gag of the awful shack (inferred) anchors this.

jokes.text: No, I don't want to stick to anything in here.
jokes.setup: Carl has told Ty to 'make yourself comfortable' in his filthy shack
jokes.punchline: Ty's flat refusal — 'I don't want to stick to anything in here' — implies the surfaces are so disgusting that physical contact would be adhesive
jokes.explanation: Economical and vivid — 'stick to anything' conjures an entire nightmare of a living space in four words. Ty's cool detachment makes it funnier than if he had said it with disgust. High quotability.

jokes.text: People say I'm an idiot or something...because all I do is cut lawns for a living. / People don't say things about you. As far as you know.
jokes.setup: Carl offers the insecure, slightly defensive claim that people call him an idiot
jokes.punchline: Ty offers what sounds like reassurance — 'People don't say things about you' — then immediately adds the devastating qualifier: 'As far as you know.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. The structure is a classic false reassurance followed by a devastating qualifier. 'As far as you know' is the knife — it confirms all Carl's worst fears while technically denying them. Ty delivering this with complete serenity makes it land harder. Highly quotable and structurally near-perfect. The economy is exceptional — four words do enormous comedic work.

jokes.text: This is registered. Carl Spackler's Bench. / ...this is a cross bluegrass, Kentucky bluegrass, featherbed bench, and northern California sinsemilla. The amazing stuff about this is that you can play 36 holes on it in the afternoon...take it home and just get stoned at night on this stuff. I've got pounds of this stuff.
jokes.setup: Carl shows Ty a grass sample, launching into what sounds like a legitimate horticultural explanation about his hybrid grass
jokes.punchline: The reveal that his hybrid grass includes 'northern California sinsemilla' (marijuana) — so the 'amazing stuff' about it is that you can golf on it AND get stoned. 'I've got pounds of this stuff' escalates from botanist to drug dealer.
jokes.explanation: Classic slow-build reveal. Carl's earnest horticultural pride runs directly into the admission that his proudest invention is partly weed. The dual-use pitch ('play 36 holes...then get stoned') is delivered with the same breathless enthusiasm as a genuine agricultural innovation. 'I've got pounds of this stuff' is a perfect kicker — it transitions from botanist to drug kingpin seamlessly. Fully earned and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: It's a little harsh. Here. Cannonball it! / Cannonball it right back... / ...then one more of these right on top of it! Cannonball coming!
jokes.setup: Carl and Ty are smoking Carl's marijuana grass hybrid; Ty finds it harsh
jokes.punchline: Carl's solution to 'a little harsh' is to 'cannonball it' — an escalating series of increasingly intense hits, culminating in a third 'cannonball coming!' suggesting Ty is now being hotboxed by an enthusiastic stoner
jokes.explanation: The escalation of 'cannonball' is funny partly because it's such an odd term of art for drug use, and partly because Ty's one-drag limit is immediately overwhelmed. Carl's enthusiasm is irrepressible. Good sustained scene comedy.

jokes.text: Can I have a drop? Just a drop... myself?
jokes.setup: Carl has been force-cannonballing Ty with increasingly intense hits of marijuana grass
jokes.punchline: Ty — the normally effortlessly cool character — meekly requests 'just a drop' for himself, suggesting the cannonballing has gotten away from him and he's now quite high
jokes.explanation: Ty reduced to a small, humble request is funny given his normal aristocratic ease. The 'just a drop...myself' delivery suggests some cognitive impairment from the cannonballing. Character-specific humor.

jokes.text: You've been acting psychotically lately.
jokes.setup: Ty and Carl are now getting high together; Ty raises a concern about Ty's own behavior (or Carl's — context suggests Ty is addressing himself or Carl)
jokes.punchline: 'Psychotically' — the clinical upgrade from 'a little odd' or 'weird' — delivered with Ty's signature unruffled calm. The fact that this observation occurs during an impulsive midnight drug session in a filthy shack adds ironic context.
jokes.explanation: Good word choice — 'psychotically' is funnier than any synonym because it's so precise and clinical. Coming from Ty, who is himself somewhat unhinged, the concern is deliciously ironic.

jokes.text: What you've got to do is cut the hamstring on the back of his leg...right at the bottom. He'll never play golf again...because his weight displacement goes back...and all his weight is on his right foot...and he'll be pushing everything off to the right. He'll never come through on anything. He'll quit the game.
jokes.setup: Ty mentions having to play Smails tomorrow; Carl offers advice about how to handle him
jokes.punchline: Carl's 'advice' is an extremely detailed plan to physically maim Smails — cutting his hamstring — with a thorough biomechanical analysis of how the injury would ruin his golf swing
jokes.explanation: One of the great Carl Spackler moments. The horror is that he's giving genuine, technically plausible advice about permanent physical injury — and the biomechanical follow-through is so detailed and earnest that it sounds like a golf instructor's tip. The escalation from 'how to handle your opponent' to 'cripple him for life' happens so naturally and confidently. 'He'll quit the game' as the closing benefit — as if leaving golf is the worst possible outcome — is a perfect dark kicker. Earns its 8+ score: it's dark, specific, character-perfect, and genuinely surprising.

jokes.text: That would work. I'm going to call you if I need that help. / But, seriously, no b.s...if you ever want to rap or just get weird with somebody. You know... buddies.
jokes.setup: Carl has just outlined a plan to permanently cripple Judge Smails
jokes.punchline: Ty's calm 'That would work' treats the maiming plan as a valid option; then Carl pivots to a touching offer of genuine friendship — 'just get weird with somebody...buddies'
jokes.explanation: Two good jokes in one beat. 'That would work' is a perfect Ty deadpan endorsement of the most violent suggestion imaginable. Then Carl's earnest bid for friendship — 'get weird with somebody...buddies' — is unexpectedly sweet and funny. 'Just get weird with somebody' is highly quotable.

jokes.text: Do you have a pool? / A pool and a pond. A pond would be good for you. Natural spring.
jokes.setup: Carl is asking about Ty's amenities as the basis for a reciprocal visit
jokes.punchline: Ty offers Carl the pond rather than the pool — 'A pond would be good for you' — a subtle classist distinction delivered with total serenity, as if assigning Carl to the outdoor, animal-adjacent option is natural
jokes.explanation: Understated and funny — Ty immediately categorizes Carl as a pond person rather than a pool person, and the qualifier 'Natural spring' is a perfect deadpan addition, as if the pond's natural provenance makes it a premium offering. Character-specific Ty comedy.

jokes.text: Thanks for the dope.
jokes.setup: Ty is leaving Carl's shack after their impromptu drug session
jokes.punchline: His parting words — 'Thanks for the dope' — are entirely sincere and casual, treating marijuana as equivalent to being thanked for a cup of tea. The phrase 'the dope' (definite article) implies a quantity was specifically provided.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words do a lot. Ty's social etiquette is impeccable even regarding controlled substances. The normalcy of the thanks is the joke. 'The dope' rather than 'some dope' is a small but good detail.

jokes.text: Get back there! What do you think you're doing? Get off of here! This is a golf course, not a parking lot! Now back this thing out of here right now!
jokes.setup: On the morning of the big match, something (a vehicle or large object belonging to Czervik's entourage) has encroached on the golf course
jokes.punchline: Smails erupts in apoplectic rage at the intrusion — his precious club is being treated like a parking lot — establishing him at maximum pomposity before the match
jokes.explanation: Standard Smails explosion. Funny because of Ted Knight's performance intensity but not especially crafted writing. 'This is a golf course, not a parking lot' is moderately quotable but generic.

jokes.text: Oh, there's my phone! / I told you never to call me on the golf course! What's that? Then sell! / They're all selling? Then buy! / I'll tell you what. Let me have the Coast. Any Coast!
jokes.setup: The match is about to begin; Czervik's phone rings
jokes.punchline: His frantic stock-trading instructions — 'sell...then buy...any Coast!' — are delivered at the first tee, treating the financial markets as the real game and golf as the sideshow
jokes.explanation: Good Czervik character work — his world is money and deals, golf is merely a venue for them. 'Any Coast!' is a good escalation. The semiotic inversion (golf course as trading floor) is funny and character-specific.

jokes.text: What do you want? / Can I use your phone? I have a call.
jokes.setup: Smails is trying to maintain order at the first tee; Czervik's phone is causing chaos
jokes.punchline: Another player (possibly the doctor) asks to use the phone — implying he also has financial dealings to attend to on the course
jokes.explanation: Quick tag joke on the phone bit — works as a minor escalation, the phone spreading like a contagion. Modest.

jokes.text: Gentlemen, we all know this is illegal and against club practice...and I'd like to ask at this time...if you all agree to waive all sanction against said referee...or anything that might get me fired.
jokes.setup: Lou is officiating a large illegal gambling match; he begins with what sounds like an official statement
jokes.punchline: His official statement is a request for personal indemnity against being fired — his only real concern is his own job security, not the legality of the match
jokes.explanation: Good institutional satire — the referee using official language to cover his own ass rather than ensure fairness. 'Anything that might get me fired' is a funny descent from legalese to blunt self-interest. Structurally solid.

jokes.text: I have a number of tees in my hand. Your Honor, odd or even? / Odd! / Odd, it is. Your honor... Your Honor.
jokes.setup: Lou calls on 'Your Honor' to call odd or even — standard coin-flip equivalent
jokes.punchline: He calls 'Your Honor' twice — the first as the standard form of address for the Judge, the second realizing/confirming that the Judge actually IS a Your Honor. It's a mild pun on the dual meaning.
jokes.explanation: Mild wordplay on the Judge's title. Gets a mild chuckle from the double-take but isn't especially sharp. Functional.

jokes.text: Don't smile at me a lot, okay?
jokes.setup: Someone in Czervik's party (possibly Czervik himself) is grinning at Smails on the tee
jokes.punchline: Smails's prissy request not to be smiled at — as if smiling were a form of aggression — reveals the depth of his petty anxieties
jokes.explanation: One of Ted Knight's best Smails moments in this reel. The specific, petty request not to be smiled at is so neurotic and character-revealing — it shows that Czervik's confidence rattles him at a visceral level. 'A lot' is a perfect qualifier — not 'don't smile at me at all,' but specifically not 'a lot,' as if one or two smiles could be tolerated. Highly quotable and very funny.

jokes.text: The Judge and Mr. Czervik have a $100,000 match going on! [caddie whispers to other caddies, spreading betting news]
jokes.setup: The match was set at $20,000, then $40,000, now a caddie announces $100,000
jokes.punchline: The number has ballooned to $100,000 through the caddie telephone — an absurd inflation of the already high stakes
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — the game-of-telephone inflation of the bet. Sets up the caddie side-betting subplot. Functional but not sharp writing.

jokes.text: Hello? Anybody home? / Hello, Mr. Gopher! It's me, Mr. Squirrel. / Just a harmless squirrel. Not a plastic explosive or anything. Nothing to be worried about. I'm just here to make your last hours on earth as peaceful as possible.
jokes.setup: Carl, disguised (or simply narrating in character), approaches the gopher hole dressed/acting as a squirrel with plastic explosives hidden on his person
jokes.punchline: His cover story — 'Not a plastic explosive or anything' — is the worst possible cover story, announcing exactly what he is hiding
jokes.explanation: Among the best pure comedy moments in this reel and the film. Carl's self-sabotaging cover story — 'Not a plastic explosive or anything. Nothing to be worried about' — is a perfect absurdist payoff on his earlier 'recruit the squirrel' strategy. The logic is completely Carl: he announces the thing he's hiding as a denial. The escalation to 'make your last hours on earth as peaceful as possible' — a hospice worker's line delivered to a gopher while holding explosives — is extraordinary dark comedy. Fully earned by the character and the setup reel pays off beautifully. Comparable to or exceeding the craft-8 anchor.

jokes.text: Or in the words of Jean-Paul Sartre... 'Au revoir, gopher.'
jokes.setup: Carl is completing his final speech to the gopher before detonating explosives
jokes.punchline: He invokes Jean-Paul Sartre — the existentialist philosopher — for the final farewell, and the 'quote' is simply 'Au revoir, gopher' — not a real Sartre quote, just French for goodbye
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in Caddyshack. Carl citing Sartre for a gopher extermination is the apex of his character's delusion of grandeur — he applies intellectual/philosophical weight to the most trivial act imaginable. The 'quote' being nothing but 'Au revoir, gopher' is the perfect anti-climax: all that Sartre buildup for a French goodbye. The gap between the highbrow citation and the bathos of the actual words is a masterclass in comedic economy. Iconic.

jokes.text: That kangaroo just stole my ball! [a kangaroo (apparent animal that wandered onto course) steals a ball]
jokes.setup: A round of golf is in progress; a ball goes wild
jokes.punchline: The ball is stolen by a kangaroo on the golf course — an absurd animal intrusion that parallels the gopher subplot
jokes.explanation: Silly visual gag — a kangaroo on a golf course. The absurdity works in the film's anarchic context. 'That kangaroo just stole my ball!' has good quotability because of its matter-of-fact delivery of an impossible scenario.

jokes.text: What's up, Doc? [Carl or another character says this to the kangaroo]
jokes.setup: A kangaroo has appeared on the golf course
jokes.punchline: The Bugs Bunny catchphrase — normally addressed to Elmer Fudd — applied to an actual kangaroo (not a rabbit), breaking the fourth wall of cartoon logic into reality
jokes.explanation: Quick pop-culture reference gag. Gets a laugh from the incongruity of Bugs Bunny's phrase addressed to a real kangaroo. Cheap but efficient.

jokes.text: Don't put yourself down, Al. / You're not... you're not good. You stink.
jokes.setup: Smails appears to offer consolation after Czervik laments playing badly — 'Don't put yourself down, Al'
jokes.punchline: He finishes the thought not with reassurance but with agreement: 'You're not...you're not good. You stink.' — the false reassurance collapses into naked honesty
jokes.explanation: Superb structural joke. The 'Don't put yourself down' setup primes the audience for a 'because you're actually good' follow-through — and instead gets blunt agreement. The stutter — 'You're not...you're not good' — mimics someone searching for the kind word before giving up. 'You stink' as the final verdict is perfectly blunt and character-specific for Smails. High quotability.

jokes.text: Fifty bucks the Smails kid picks his nose.
jokes.setup: Spaulding (Smails's nephew) is lining up a shot; Czervik is watching
jokes.punchline: Instead of commenting on the golf, Czervik is betting on Spaulding picking his nose — a child-focused gross-out bet placed with the same casual confidence as a stock tip
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of the absolute confidence in Czervik's read on the kid — he's already categorized Spaulding as a nose-picker with betting certainty. The casualness of the fifty-dollar bet (small relative to the main match) mirrors the casual cruelty. Sets up a perfect payoff.

jokes.text: Fifty bucks more says he eats it.
jokes.setup: Czervik's initial bet that Spaulding picks his nose is apparently paying off (someone presumably gives the signal)
jokes.punchline: He immediately escalates to the next logical gross-out level — eating it — with another fifty-dollar bet placed at the precise moment of maximum disgust
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat escalation. Having established the nose-pick as a known Spaulding behavior, the logical and disgusting escalation to eating it arrives exactly on cue. The betting structure gives it a formal rhythm. 'Fifty bucks more' maintains the casual financial framing. Excellent setup-payoff structure over just two beats.

jokes.text: Don't do it, kid! [Smails, apparently watching in horror, implores Spaulding not to eat it]
jokes.setup: Czervik has bet $50 that Spaulding eats his booger; Smails has heard the bet
jokes.punchline: Smails breaks into the scene to desperately plead with his own nephew — not to protect the child's dignity but to prevent Czervik from winning the bet, or simply from pure patrician horror
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the bet sequence — Smails's horror and the futility of his plea add to the humiliation. Character-specific in the right way.

jokes.text: That kid will eat anything! / He was hungry.
jokes.setup: Spaulding has apparently eaten his booger as predicted; Czervik reacts
jokes.punchline: The deadpan reply — 'He was hungry' — offers the most reductive possible explanation, as if this were simply a hunger issue
jokes.explanation: 'He was hungry' is a perfect deadpan kicker. Three words that offer a straight-faced, completely inadequate explanation for a deeply gross event. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Hey, Judge, cheer up, will you? My boat needs exactly $20,000 worth of repairs.
jokes.setup: The match is going badly for the Smails team; Czervik tries to cheer the Judge up
jokes.punchline: His idea of comfort is reminding Smails that Czervik needs his winnings for boat repairs — i.e., the $20,000 Smails is about to lose is already earmarked for Czervik's yacht
