jokes.explanation: Czervik's trolling disguised as sympathy — 'cheer up' followed immediately by news of how he'll spend the money he takes from you. The specificity of '$20,000 worth of boat repairs' is funny because it's so casually exact. Character-specific vulgarian comedy.

jokes.text: So does your brain! You want to double it?
jokes.setup: Czervik has told Smails his boat needs $20,000 in repairs
jokes.punchline: Smails fires back that Czervik's brain needs repairs too, and in his rage doubles the bet
jokes.explanation: The insult is average but the bet-doubling consequence of his rage is good — Smails's temper keeps digging him deeper. Structurally nice that the escalation is emotion-driven.

jokes.text: Probably just a routine emergency.
jokes.setup: Czervik has just been called away (his phone rings or his office calls) and he tries to downplay it while locked into an $80,000 bet
jokes.punchline: 'Probably just a routine emergency' — a perfect oxymoron delivered with Czervik's breezy confidence, treating a potential crisis as a standard inconvenience
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the reel. 'Routine emergency' is an oxymoron that perfectly captures Czervik's frenetic life — emergencies are so frequent they've become routine. The delivery makes it funnier — total nonchalance about something that sounds alarming. Highly quotable and extremely economical.

jokes.text: Why did I double it? I should have stayed home and played with myself!
jokes.setup: Smails has just doubled the bet in a rage, raising it to $80,000; he is now alone and second-guessing himself
jokes.punchline: 'I should have stayed home and played with myself!' — an accidental innuendo that Smails delivers in complete sincerity, meaning he should have played a solo round of golf
jokes.explanation: Classic accidental double-entendre — 'played with myself' means solo golf but sounds like masturbation. What makes it land especially well is that Smails says it in tortured sincerity, without any awareness of the other meaning, which is entirely in character for the repressed stuffed-shirt Judge. Good quotability.

jokes.text: I saw Smails before. He was cheating. / Nobody likes a tattletale... except, of course, me.
jokes.setup: Someone reports that Smails was cheating
jokes.punchline: Czervik breaks the conventional 'nobody likes a tattletale' cliché mid-sentence: '...except, of course, me.' — instantly valorizing tattling when it benefits him
jokes.explanation: Smart subversion of a tired cliché. Czervik starts the expected wisdom and then immediately carves out his own exception, revealing his entirely self-interested moral framework. '...except, of course, me' has perfect timing and rhythm. Highly quotable and very character-specific.

jokes.text: Oh! My arm! It's broken! / What has this buffoon done now?
jokes.setup: During the match, something happens to Dr. Beeper that injures his arm (Czervik's cart or club bag presumably causes the injury)
jokes.punchline: The slapstick injury itself, plus Smails's reaction — 'What has this buffoon done now?' — framing the injury as another Czervik inconvenience rather than a medical emergency
jokes.explanation: Setup slapstick for the forfeit/substitution plot turn. 'What has this buffoon done now?' is good Smails-speak but the injury itself is fairly generic physical comedy. Functional.

jokes.text: I'm afraid you forfeit. / Who says so? The match is a draw! / You don't play, you lose. Right, Lou? / That's right, unless you allow him a substitute.
jokes.setup: The doctor's injury means Smails's team can't complete the match
jokes.punchline: Smails's desperate attempt to call it a draw — 'The match is a draw!' — is immediately shot down by Czervik, then Lou introduces the substitute option, which is the actual plot engine
jokes.explanation: More plot machinery than comedy, but Smails's instant 'The match is a draw!' — trying to unilaterally declare a result that suits him — is funny in its brazenness.

jokes.text: Who do you want? / Sonja Henie is out. We'll take Danny Noonan.
jokes.setup: Czervik gets to pick the substitute player for Smails's team
jokes.punchline: He rules out the famously graceful skater Sonja Henie ('Sonja Henie is out') — implying he considered her — before selecting Danny. The gag is the implied absurd shortlist.
jokes.explanation: Good throwaway joke — the implication that Czervik seriously considered a 1950s figure skater for the substitute and had to rule her out is funny in its absurdism. Economy is excellent. The anachronism adds to the silliness.

jokes.text: Makes a lot of sense. / If you win, I'll make it worth your while.
jokes.setup: Smails has objected that Danny is an employee and can't play in an illegal match; Ty dismisses the objection
jokes.punchline: 'Makes a lot of sense' as pure deadpan sarcasm — Smails's objection is the least of anyone's concerns given the illegal nature of the whole event
jokes.explanation: Light Ty sarcasm, functional. The 'worth your while' motivation of Danny is more plot than joke.

jokes.text: I'll play. / You don't want that scholarship, do you? / I guess I don't. / I guess you don't!
jokes.setup: Danny agrees to play in the illegal match against Smails, essentially burning his chance at the scholarship Smails controls
jokes.punchline: Smails's smug 'I guess you don't!' — gleeful that Danny has just destroyed his own prospects — is a satisfying character moment revealing Smails's pettiness as his defining trait
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of this exchange — particularly 'I guess I don't / I guess you don't!' — has good comedic timing. Smails's glee at Danny's self-defeat is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Don't worry. It's good luck. / In Haiti!
jokes.setup: Someone does something (presumably a minor incident — bird dropping, or a similar bad omen) and reassures the Judge it's good luck
jokes.punchline: Smails's dry correction: 'In Haiti!' — suggesting that whatever just happened is only considered good luck in a specific remote location
jokes.explanation: Two words do a lot of work. 'In Haiti!' is a perfect kicker — specific enough to be funny, geographically arbitrary enough to be absurd. Great economy. The specificity of choosing Haiti (rather than a generic 'somewhere else') is the key detail.

jokes.text: You've got to win this hole. / I kind of thought winning wasn't important. / Me winning isn't! You do! / Great grammar.
jokes.setup: Ty has been coaching Danny with Zen anti-competitive philosophy all film; now he urgently needs Danny to win
jokes.punchline: His attempted distinction — 'Me winning isn't! You do!' — is both grammatically scrambled and an admission that his philosophy was always self-serving. Danny's 'Great grammar' is a perfect straight-man kicker.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in this reel — a perfect character payoff. All of Ty's 'winning isn't everything' philosophy collapses the moment his money is on the line, and his desperate grammatically-broken backpedal ('Me winning isn't! You do!') exposes the hypocrisy perfectly. Danny's dry 'Great grammar' is a beautiful straight-man kicker that refuses to let Ty off the hook. The callback to Ty's philosophy earns maximum points. Comparable to the craft-8 anchor and justified.

jokes.text: See your future. Be... your future. Make... make it! / Make your future. I'm a veg, Danny.
jokes.setup: Ty is trying to give Danny pre-shot motivational instructions
jokes.punchline: His motivational speech deteriorates into incoherence — 'Make... make it!' — and concludes with the admission 'I'm a veg, Danny,' suggesting he is too high from Carl's grass to function properly
jokes.explanation: A delayed callback to the drug session — Ty is now visibly impaired and his coaching has degraded to 'I'm a veg.' The escalating dissolution of his Zen coaching into vegetative stoner confession is a perfect character moment. 'I'm a veg, Danny' is extremely quotable. The callback adds significant value.

jokes.text: Spaulding, this calls for the old Billy Baroo. [Smails retrieves a special putter with ceremony]
jokes.setup: Spaulding needs to sink a critical putt; Smails treats it as a moment for his legendary putter
jokes.punchline: The invocation of 'the old Billy Baroo' — a named putter treated like a legendary weapon — combined with the pompous ceremony of its deployment, is comedy through over-escalation
jokes.explanation: The name 'Billy Baroo' is intrinsically funny — it sounds like a novelty item, not a champion's implement. Smails deploying it with the gravity of Excalibur being drawn from stone is perfect character inflation. Very quotable. Sets up the callback payoff.

jokes.text: This is a biggy! Don't let me down, Billy! Forty thousand dollars... Billy!
jokes.setup: Smails is imploring his putter 'Billy Baroo' to perform on the critical putt
jokes.punchline: He addresses the putter directly — 'Don't let me down, Billy!' — as a person with agency, then reminds the putter of the financial stakes: 'Forty thousand dollars...Billy!'
jokes.explanation: Smails's relationship with his putter has escalated to co-dependent — he's now motivating it with the financial stakes. 'Forty thousand dollars...Billy!' is a great kicker because it treats the putter as a business partner who needs to understand the gravity of the situation. The pause before 'Billy' is key. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I knew you'd do it! [Smails celebrating the made putt with Billy Baroo]
jokes.setup: Smails has begged and implored Billy Baroo; the putt goes in
jokes.punchline: His immediate vindication — 'I knew you'd do it!' — addressed to the putter, treating the inanimate object as having chosen to perform
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the Billy Baroo bit — his faith in the putter was rewarded, and he treats it as a personal relationship. Diminishing returns on the bit but still charming.

jokes.text: Don't worry about this one. If you miss it, we lose.
jokes.setup: Ty is trying to calm Danny before the decisive putt
jokes.punchline: 'Don't worry about this one' is reassurance; 'If you miss it, we lose' is the precise opposite — the most pressure-inducing statement possible — delivered with Ty's same airy calm
jokes.explanation: One of the great Ty Webb jokes and a highlight of the film. The structure is flawless: reassurance immediately contradicted by the most high-stakes caveat imaginable, with zero change in Ty's tone. 'Don't worry about this one. If you miss it, we lose.' is a perfect ten-word bit that could only come from Ty — a character who operates in a reality adjacent to but separate from the one everyone else inhabits. Exceptional economy (10 words, enormous payload), structure-perfect, and entirely character-specific. Earns its score.

jokes.text: Hey, Judge! Double or nothing he makes it! Eighty thousand dollars!
jokes.setup: Danny is about to putt for the whole match; Czervik impulsively raises the stakes one more time
jokes.punchline: Czervik cannot resist betting even when he's already winning — 'double or nothing he makes it!' — revealing pathological gambling instincts that override all strategic thinking
jokes.explanation: Czervik's compulsive bet-raising is a good character beat — he's found something he loves more than money, which is the action itself. Functional escalation.

jokes.text: It's a birdie! [Danny's ball goes in after appearing to miss — delayed drop into the cup]
jokes.setup: The ball appeared to miss (lips out, or pauses on the edge), earning Smails's taunt; everyone thinks it's over
jokes.punchline: The ball drops in — a delayed, improbable made putt that reverses the entire situation in an instant
jokes.explanation: High impact because of the cumulative narrative investment — this pays off Danny's entire arc and Smails's premature taunt simultaneously. Not craft-heavy but delivers significant emotional and comedic impact as a structural/plot payoff.

jokes.text: All right, Smails, that's 80 grand. Now fork it over! / I'll give you nothing! Absolutely nothing, you understand! / I figured as much! Hey, Moose! Rocco! Help the judge find his checkbook.
jokes.setup: Czervik has won $80,000 and demands payment; Smails refuses with maximum indignation
jokes.punchline: Czervik, anticipating exactly this refusal — 'I figured as much!' — immediately summons his enforcer muscle: Moose and Rocco, to 'help the judge find his checkbook'
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy — Czervik is rich enough to have mob-adjacent 'assistants' named Moose and Rocco, and his elegant euphemism 'help the judge find his checkbook' is a great piece of comic understatement for what is implied physical intimidation. 'I figured as much' shows he knew Smails would renege, adding prescience to his character. Good final beat.

jokes.text: I figured as much! Hey, Moose! Rocco! Help the judge find his checkbook.
jokes.setup: Smails has refused to pay; Czervik anticipated this
jokes.punchline: Czervik immediately produces 'Moose' and 'Rocco' — mob-connected heavies — to 'help' Smails find his checkbook. The euphemism 'help him find his checkbook' for extortion is a great gangster-movie parody.
jokes.explanation: Great reveal — Czervik has mob associates named Moose and Rocco, which explains (retroactively) how he got to be this wealthy. The euphemism 'help him find his checkbook' is a perfect gangster-speak joke. 'I figured as much' establishes Czervik knew Smails wouldn't pay — further cementing his street-smart vs. Smails' WASP-bluster dynamic.

jokes.text: Well, I, uh... oh, I will. [Smails folds immediately upon seeing Moose and Rocco]
jokes.setup: Smails has defiantly refused to pay; Czervik has summoned Moose and Rocco
jokes.punchline: Smails's instant capitulation — 'Well, I, uh... oh, I will' — his entire resistance collapsing the moment physical consequences appear. The 'oh, I will' as a resigned acceptance is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The speed of his fold is the joke — all that pomposity and 'absolutely nothing!' evaporates instantly. The stammering 'Well, I, uh...' followed by the resigned 'oh, I will' is a perfect character comedic beat. Ted Knight's physical performance presumably sells this enormously.

jokes.text: Hey, everybody! We're all going to get laid!
jokes.setup: The match is won and payment secured; everyone is waiting for Czervik's victory declaration
jokes.punchline: Instead of a golf victory speech, Czervik's announcement is purely carnal: 'We're all going to get laid!' — the ultimate Czervik: money, winning, and sex as the only metrics that matter
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing Czervik line — loud, vulgar, euphoric, completely in character. The public announcement to everyone present ('Hey, everybody!') makes it maximally inappropriate and therefore maximally funny. As a topper for the reel's climax, it works well. High quotability.
